2.2 The Customer Lifecycle
Let’s review the customer lifecycle before we dive too deeply into strategy since it will serve as the basis for a lot of the concepts in this book. A typical customer lifecycle consists of five parts: awareness, acquisition, engagement, activation, and retention. The journey through the conversion funnel is not always linear and could jump stages. For example, an individual might use a product (acquisition), get tired of the product and contemplate abandoning it (retention), and fall back in love with the product (engagement). Notwithstanding what journey an individual might take, we need to have a game plan for each stage.
2.2.1 Customer Awareness
It all starts with awareness. One study performed by McKinsey & Company indicated thatit can take five to eight exposures to an advertisement for it to make people truly aware of a product. People can learn about your product in many different ways such as through traditional marketing, through friends and acquaintances, and through organic news stories. What might be less obvious to the reader is that the product itself can help spread awareness. For example, a social sharing feature can help current customers recommend your product to your friends. Your operations can affect awareness too. For example, your customers can learn about new products that your company is offering when they call customer support.
2.2.2 Customer Acquisition
After a person learns about your product, they might decide that they want to try or buy it. This begins the acquisition period. It might seem that acquisition should not be a phase but rather a short point in time, but that is rarely how people become customers. For mobile apps, a new user might have to sign up. That can be a long and complex process involving filling out a registration form, validating their email, and completing their profile. Potential customers can leave the acquisition cycle in any of those steps, and it is not until they get through the whole process before they become active customers.
For other products such as enterprise software, the acquisition process can be extremely drawn out and can involve a sales team that pitches the product, a technical implementation team that helps to answer technical questions and sets up the product, a training team, and so on. The acquisition phase starts with the intent to try or buy a product and ends when the customer actually buys the product or uses the product for the first time.
2.2.3 Customer Engagement
Just because a person has used or bought your product does not mean that they are a valuable customer. Even popular apps like Twitter have scores of users that post a few things and then never use it again. Those are not engaged users, and having unengaged users is bad for business. Usually customers fail to become engaged because they either can’t overcome the learning curve or the product fails to meet their expectations. Luckily, it’s possible to systematically and predictably fix both.
Some products have much more compressed engagement cycles. For example, if you are in the market for a luxury yacht, you probably won’t be making a bunch of repeat purchases. However, that does not mean that all yacht owners are equally engaged. Some owners love their luxury yachts, and it shows as they merrily sail around the Mediterranean and extol their yacht’s virtues to their friends. Those are the kinds of customers that you want!
2.2.4 Customer Activation
Activation is a big jump in the customer’s level of engagement. The anecdote that I like to tell is my relationship with Amazon. I became an Amazon customer in 2001, when I was a college student. I realized that buying textbooks on Amazon could save me a ton of money, so every term I bought a bunch of books on Amazon. I was a pretty engaged customer. I liked that I could save money, which was tight during my college years, and I was generally happy with the service.
Fast forward a few more years, and Amazon’s offerings broadened. At that point, I was a young professional, and I would occasionally buy a DVD or a book. Once again, I was a solid repeat customer, but I would only buy things that were difficult to track down in a physical store and for which I could wait a week to be delivered. I still preferred to run down to my local BestBuy to buy electronics, DVDs and videogames since I could get it right away.
Fast forward again to 2009 when I went back to graduate school, and Amazon gave me a free Amazon Prime membership since I was a student. That year I bought my textbooks on Amazon, but my purchase behavior started to change radically. Suddenly, I was buying everything on Amazon: DVDs, video games, electronics, clothes, household items, you name it. On reflection, my Amazon Prime subscription annihilated a huge deterrent: having to wait a week for my orders. I didn’t realize at the time what a big roadblock the shipping time was, but now that I had free two-day shipping the floodgates were open. In fact, there was a time when my sons were still babies, when I’d get Amazon shipments multiple times a week filled with diapers, baby clothes, household items. That is what I call Activation!
Activation is a phase in a customer’s lifetime when they become super engaged. Many customers never get to that stage, but that is where the biggest growth can happen.
2.2.5 Customer Retention
Unfortunately, all good things must come to an end. Even your most activated customers may get frustrated with your product or company and will choose to leave at some point. More likely, those customers that never got very engaged will abandon your product. The good news is that abandonment does not usually happen instantaneously. There are often signs that a customer is unhappy, and you will likely have ample opportunities to make your customers happy. Even better, you can take steps during customer acquisition and engagement that will prevent your customers from becoming unhappy with your product once they convert to active customers.
I was recently trying a new online project management app. The app and the company behind it did many things right to make sure that I would not get frustrated or disappointed as I became an active user. First, when I signed up for the app, they sent me a personalized email from an individual on their team thanking me for registering and letting me know that I can contact her at any point if I have any questions or issues. Second, when I logged onto the app for the first time, they had a great video tutorial giving me an overview of the features and best practices. On top of that, they had little contextual tutorial messages as I explored the app for the first time.
I set up a simple project to test out the software and invited one of my teammates. It was a pretty solid project management app, but there were a few little things that irked me, and I stopped using it with time. The company saw that I hadn’t used it in a while and they sent me a couple emails (automated, I’m sure, but signed by my customer service representative) asking me if there is anything that they can do to help me with the app. I finally relented and replied to the email and set up a call with my dedicated customer service representative that addressed each of my complaints in turn. She couldn’t solve all of them, but she did help me find other ways to get things done. The company not only did its best to avoid abandonment, but they also successfully retained me when I was not totally happy. I’m still a loyal customer.
2.2.6 Engagement Versus Retention
Not everyone will agree with defining retention as simply a measure of keeping customers. To some retention means the act of keeping customers coming back, while engagement is a measure of how intensely they use your product at any one time. For example, they would consider Google Search to be a product with low engagement and high retention given that users use Google Search briefly, but then keep coming back.
Consider a student that is writing a term paper, who uses Google to help them find resources and information, and then never uses Google again. Because they were doing a ton of queries while writing the term paper, we would say that their engagement was high but their retention was low because they never used Google again. I think the majority of people would not consider this person to be highly engaged even if they did submit dozens of searches in a day. Wikipedia users are similar. They use the online encyclopedia intensively but infrequently.
I find it more useful to think of engagement as a measure of how much a customer is using a product, which is a function of intensity and frequency, whereas retention indicates if I am still an active customer. For example, which user is most engaged, one that uses your product once every day or another that uses your product ten times a day every ten days? What about a customer that uses your product twenty times over the span of two days but never touches it again? I would say that the user that used it twenty times and never again is not engaged because he is not an active customer while the other two are roughly equally engaged.
It’s often very ambiguous whether to consider some customers as being active or having abandoned your product, and every company has it’s own cutoff point depending on the nature of your product. For example, many years ago, I signed up for Flickr to share my photos with friends and family but stopped using it after a while and have not logged on for over four years. I still have an account, so am I still an active Flickr customer? It depends on Flickr’s definition of what they consider to be an “active customer.”
2.2.7 How Acquisition, Engagement, Retention Work Together
In 2007, a recent Yale graduate, Justin Kan, came up with an idea to stream every minute of his life over the internet. With the help of Emmett Shear, Michael Seibel and Kyle Vogt, he created Justin.tv, which would become the world’s first prominent livecasting service. The team grew Justin.tv to be a fairly solid business employing about twenty-five people, but at some point thefounders realized that their idea had hit a ceiling. There were only so many things that it made sense to livecast, and they had tapped out all of them.
Justin.tv rose to about 30 million unique visitors per month, but the majority of their users weren’t super engaged, except for one tiny segment. Emmett Shear made the realization that video gamers, which made up just 3% of their user base, were fanatical users. They would sometimes spend hours streaming themselves playing video games and others would watch them playing for long stretches of time. The four founders decided to focus on addressing just the video game market and created a new version of Justin.tv called Twitch, which became one of the hottest startups in Silicon Valley and sold to Amazon for $970 million.
Justin.tv had the perfect product all along, but they were distributing it to the wrong customer base. Not too many people were super engaged by watching Justin sleep or others sit around in front of the computer, but the video gamers were completely hooked. Once they focused on acquiring the video gamers their product growth exploded. This is one of the best examples of how acquisition, engagement, and retention are related.
Many people forget that the concept of product-market fit is composed of two parts and focus, instead, on just the product. However, it’s not just about building the perfect product. Finding the right customer whose needs your product meets most adeptly is just as important.
If you target the wrong customer, it does not matter how good your product is, you will always have problems engaging those customers because they won’t really have the problem that your product is trying to solve. It’s like selling goose down parkas in Miami Beach. You might have the most stylish, warmest goose down parka in the world, but if you sell it to folks in a place that is constantly hot, your customers won’t love your product and will eventually shove it in their closet or give it away to Goodwill. On the other hand, if you sold that same amazing down parka in St. Paul, Minnesota, your customers would wear it all winter long and would love it for years to come. Their engagement and retention would be off the charts.
To put it simply, if you are effectively targeting and acquiring the right customers for your product, they will appreciate it and will be highly engaged. Customers that are highly engaged, are very unlikely to abandon your product. How much do you like Google? I bet you’re a highly engaged Google user. Are you very likely to stop using Google. Probably not unless another even more amazing search engine comes along.
2.2.8 Key Points in the Customer Lifecycle
At the beginning and end of each phase of the conversion funnel are key events that demarcate the end of one and the beginning of another. These points are hugely important because you can influence these events to supercharge your growth.
The First Time Someone Hears About or Sees Your Product
A good first impression is trickier than you might think, and it will set the stage for the rest of your relationship with you customer. First, you want to make sure that you’re reaching the right people — those that have the problem that your product is solving. You also want to make sure to communicate how your product is better at meeting their needs or solving their problems. Finally, you should tell them how to get your product or what to do next. Without meeting these three fundamental awareness goals, acquisition becomes an uphill battle. Even engagement, activation and retention can be adversely affected by a poor first impression.
The First Time Someone Uses or Buys Your Product
Usability and customer onboarding make the biggest difference when it comes to creating a great first experience. There is not much that you can do if your product doesn’t have the right features to meet the needs of a customer. Certainly, you can add important missing features with time, but by that time many of the dissatisfied customers will be long gone. Not only that, as soon as you add a new feature, customers will want others, and you will be constantly playing catchup. However, I have found that for a significant set of the customers the right features do exist, but they are hard to find or understand how to use. Moreover, bad usability often forces customers to abandon products long before they learn their full utility. Both of these problems are preventable, and addressing them will go an extremely long way to improving your engagement and retention.
The Customer Uses Your Product More or Buys More
A user will very rarely discover how great your product is in their first use. It often takes many interactions to find out if and how well it will work for the customer. Using or buying a new product is an awful lot like moving to a new city. It takes a while to learn where the good restaurants, parks, and hangout spots are.
Often times we are pleasantly surprised about what the city has to offer. Other times we are disappointed to find that there is not much more to the new place than initially meets the eye. It’s not that the place has changed in the time since you moved; you just have learned it more deeply. Often people discover new things with the help of their friends or colleagues. With your product, you want to be that friend that guides their discovery. Your marketing, product, and operations should be aimed at helping the user discover and learn your product as quickly as possible, so they appreciate it for what it really is.
Customer Becomes a Habitual User or Buyer
The holy grail of growth is the point at which an individual becomes a habitual user or buyer. This is when they enter the activated phase of their customer lifetime. We all are very familiar with this concept. Earlier, I told my story about how Amazon was able to activate me, though free two-day shipping, to become a weekly shopper. If you are on Facebook, you are very likely a habitual user, checking your account at least a few times per week.
On the other hand, there are also many products that I use sporadically. For example, there is a personal finance software that I have been using for the past five years, but I only log onto it when my spending really gets out of hand. According to many reports, there are a great number of Twitter users that are like that. Folks sign up, write a few tweets, follow a few users and then hardly do anything else. On the other hand, there are many Twitter users that post seemingly every minute. The latter are the kinds of customers you want to cultivate with great product experiences, effective marketing, and world-class operations.
Customer Becomes Unhappy with Your Product
Even the best products in the world have unhappy customers. For example, theaverage customer satisfaction score in the United States is 87%. That means that about 13% of customers are unhappy at any one time. If your product is a social media app, your customer satisfaction score is likely around 78%.
Disappointment and frustration can be factor of both product experience as well as marketing. You can have the best financial management tool in the world for middle income customers, but if you have high net worth or very poor customers, they will likely become unhappy with your product. On the other hand, you could be reaching the perfect audience, but perhaps your product is difficult to use. This will also not work in your favor.
There are also times when customers simply haven’t been able to figure out how to use your product to truly meet their needs. Luckily, that’s something that you can fix by systematically listening to your customers, experimenting with better ways to help them get the best of your product, measuring the impact that those changes have, and keeping only those that move the needle in the right direction.
Individual Stops Using the Product
Social scientists believe that the last impression is more important than the first. That is why you should make sure to end on a good note as much as you can. If you can do a good job saying goodbye to a customer, you might still get them back in the future. Perhaps they stopped using your product because it was missing a key feature, and when you finally build that feature you want them to try it again! Just as importantly, ending on a good note might mean that they will refer your product to their friends and colleagues. The might say, “It didn’t have this one thing that I really wanted, but it’s still a great product and a caring company!”
2.2.9 Marketing, Product, Operations through the Customer Lifecycle
Marketing, product design, and operations can each affect all stages of the customer lifecycle. It’s obvious that marketing can drive awareness, but we also saw with the above examples that product features and even customer support can drive awareness as well as acquisition. Conversely, how good a business is at turning interested folks into customers depends greatly on their ability to market to and draw the right customer. It is important to remember that marketing, product implementation, and operations could potentially affect all parts of the customer lifecycle as we consider how to engineer growth.

title: Understanding Primary Sales and Secondary Sales and How They Balance Demand and Supply | by Sarah Annisa | Medium

Understanding Primary Sales and Secondary Sales and How They Balance Demand and Supply
There are two main types of sales activities: Primary Sales and Secondary Sales. See how it affects your product demand and supply.
Let’s start by understandingPrimary Sales. Primary Sales refer to the selling activities conducted by a company directly to its buyers. In the FMCG or manufacturing industry, these buyers often act as distributors who then distribute the products to customers through various retail outlets such as supermarkets, minimarkets, and provisions stores. Primary Sales help us measure the number of products sold on a given day. However, when it comes to predicting current and future sales potential, we should pay more attention to Secondary Sales.
Secondary Salesare closely linked to Primary Sales. It refers to the selling activities that occur between our direct buyers (distributors) and the end customers. This can involve selling the products through retail stores or directly to the consumers themselves. Let’s consider an example: our company produces and sells chocolates. We sell chocolates to distributors who then supply them to supermarkets in town. This initial sale to the distributor is classified as Primary Sales. When the distributor sells the chocolates to the supermarket owner, it is categorized as Secondary Sales.
In smaller industries, Secondary Sales can sometimes occur directly between the distributor and the consumer, without the need for intermediate stores. Let’s say we are selling cakes in a home industry setting. A cake chef, like a housewife running her business from home, sells cakes to a bakery and pastry store. This is considered Primary Sales. When the bakery and pastry store then sells the cakes to individual consumers, it becomes Secondary Sales.
Now, why should we care about Secondary Sales?
Why is it important to define and track our selling activities? Maintaining a focus on Secondary Sales provides insights into consumer demand, helps us predict our progress, estimate future sales, and develop strategies to enhance brand awareness for our products. Let’s consider a scenario: if we sell 5 apples in Primary Sales, but only 3 apples are sold in Secondary Sales, what can we conclude? Clearly, our product is not generating significant demand in the market. In such cases, we might consider reducing the number of apples we sell in the future. On the other hand, if we sell 5 apples in Primary Sales, but there is a demand for 10 apples in Secondary Sales, what should we do? We should increase our apple supply to meet the demand in Secondary Sales.
Keep them balanced as much as possible
These two types of selling can lead to two different outcomes:
Firstly, if Primary Sales exceed Secondary Sales, it indicates that our product is less desirable in the market. This has negative implications, such as excess stock in stores and, worst of all, a potential reduction in future orders from our distributors. Imagine if we supply 100 candies to a store in Primary Sales, but only 30 candies are purchased by consumers in Secondary Sales. In such a situation, the store is unlikely to request more candy supplies from us since our candies would continue to pile up on their shelves.
Secondly, if Secondary Sales exceed Primary Sales, is it a good thing? Not necessarily. While it signifies high demand compared to supply, we need to consider the availability of our product in stores. Let’s say we supply 50 candies to a store in Primary Sales, but consumers require 150 candies based on actual sales. This would lead to an out-of-stock (OOS) condition. Remember, consumers are king, and they won’t wait indefinitely. To avoid an OOS condition, we must be prepared to produce and stock more candies quickly. Delaying this could result in consumers switching to competitor candies.
Ideally, there should be a balance between Primary and Secondary Sales. Although we don’t live in a perfect world, we can strive to minimize the significant gap between these two types of sales.
Wrap up
In conclusion, understanding the dynamics between Primary Sales and Secondary Sales is crucial for effectively managing product demand and supply. While Primary Sales give us insights into immediate sales figures, it is Secondary Sales that provide valuable information about consumer demand and future sales potential. By maintaining a balance between these two types of sales, businesses can optimize their inventory, predict sales trends, and develop strategies to meet customer expectations. It is essential to track and analyze both Primary and Secondary Sales to make informed decisions and stay competitive in the market.

Recursive BOM with Routing in Manufacturing
Recursive BOM with Routing in Manufacturing
The🇺🇸Manufacturing is Coming Back, but…
What are the Real Bottlenecks for Manufacturing
Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems are at the heart of modern manufacturing — yet one of their most critical features often becomes their greatest bottleneck:the Bill of Materials (BOM).
In manufacturing, aBOMis a hierarchical list of components and subcomponents required to build a finished product. It’s essentially a blueprint of how things are put together — from nuts and bolts, all the way to final assemblies.
Equally important is therouting: the sequence of operations required to transform raw materials into a finished good. Each routing step — likecutting,drilling,welding, orpolishing— adds time, cost, and complexity to production.
Take the metal hardware manufacturing as an example…
Ever wonder what causes themostproduct complaints at Louis Vuitton repair centers?
Surprisingly, it’s thesnap hookof the boutique bags— a small part that breaks more often than you’d think.
Routings can be particularly tricky:
Weldingoperations may have lower yield rates due to precision challenges
Polishingmight require repeated passes for quality assurance
Heat treatmentcan cause dimensional changes, requiring rework or scrap
These realities aren’t always captured cleanly in ERP systems, especially in platforms likeSAP Business One (SAP B1)which offer basic BOM support but lack deep recursive analytics or built-in routing cost calculations.
That’s where integration comes in: by combiningBOM hierarchywithrouting details, we can compute:
Total raw material quantities needed (including nested levels)
Labor and machine time per component
Process-specific cost per finished unit
Yield-adjusted material planning
Such analysis solves real operational pain points:
Prevents over-ordering of raw materials
Identifies high-cost operations in the process chain
Improves quotation accuracy
Enables predictive scheduling and resource allocation
During my time at a global metal manufacturing subsidiary, I tackled this exact challenge — building a recursive BOM + routing analysis engine from the ground up. I believe the approach would help those companies with limited resources and budget.
The First Challenge: BOM Expansion in SAP
Unlike flat BOMs used in simple manufacturing,SAP stores Bills of Materials (BOMs) as hierarchical trees. Each finished good (FG) may consist of subassemblies (SFGs), which in turn have multiple raw materials, each with its own quantities.

Recursive Structures and Mathematical Thinking

At its core, this recursive BOM expansion is atree traversal problem— every finished product (FG) is the root of a tree, and each semi-finished product (SFG) or material is a node, linked by “parent-child” relationships with quantity multipliers.

Tree-based Dynamic Programming:Where solutions are built bottom-up or top-down
Matrix Chain Multiplication (in reverse):Where the cumulative impact is multiplicative across ordered nodes
Thetrickiestpart was not the SQL syntax, but:
Ensuring that shared components (used by multiple FGs) didn’t double-count
Preventing cyclic dependencies (rare but possible in poorly maintained BOMs)
Handling deep trees (up to 11 layers!) within time limits in ETL runs
This was not just a data problem. It was agraph problem under business constraints.

Why Pentaho Was Limiting — And How I’d Rebuild It + Routing Synergy
While Pentaho served well as an introductory ETL tool, it fell short when scaling to complexmulti-tier integrations between BOM and Routing structures.
In a robust manufacturing intelligence system, understandingwhat materials are needed (BOM)is only half the equation. You also need to knowhow they are processed (Routing)— each routing step adds cost, labor, and time.
The Integrated BOM-Routing Model
In SAP B1 and similar ERP systems, two key tables underpin production planning:
BOM Table (OITT + ITT1): defines which components go into a parent item, including quantities
Routing Table (OITT joined with OWOR + WOR1): defineshowthe item is produced, with steps including work centers, standard times, and cost centers
To computetotal cost and time, I constructed an integrated model where each semi-finished item (SFG) would:
Be expanded recursively using BOM logic
For each node (item), retrieve the routing sequence (StepID,OperationCode)

Costing per routing step is multiplied at each layer and summed upwards
How I’d Rebuild It Today (Modern Stack)
If I were to rebuild this system today, I would:

Lessons from Refactoring
Rebuilding this solution in Python has revealed a powerful truth:the right tools don’t just make systems faster — they make teams stronger.
When we first implemented this usingPentaho, it gave us a quick win with its visual ETL workflow. But over time, we faced growing limitations:
Complex recursive logic was visually fragmented across multiple jobs
Query time ballooned as BOM depth increased
Version control was weak; debugging a pipeline often meant opening 5+ transformation files

💡Switching to Python changed everything.

Most importantly, theteam could now fully own and improve the codebase— it was no longer a mystery locked inside a GUI.
Looking Forward
Though our Python-based ETL proved highly effective, several advanced options are now within reach:

What is Work Order? Six Step Guide to Create an Effective Work Orders
Often overlooked, work orders are the unsung heroes ensuring that tasks are executed efficiently, resources are allocated optimally, and teams collaborate seamlessly. But what exactly is a work order? Why is it so crucial, and how can organizations harness its full potential? Dive into this comprehensive guide as we unravel the world of work orders, from their fundamental essence to the modern tools that elevate their capabilities. Whether you’re a seasoned operations manager or just stepping into the realm of maintenance management, this guide promises insights that will enhance your understanding and optimize your processes.
What is a Work Order?
A work order is a formalized document that provides specific instructions for a maintenance, repair, or operational task. It acts as a communication tool between departments, ensuring that tasks are clearly defined, authorized, and tracked from initiation to completion. Work orders may contain the following details,
Task Details: A clear description of the job.
Assigned Personnel: Who is responsible for executing the task.
Time Frame: When the task should start and its expected completion date.
Resources Needed: Any tools, parts, or equipment required.
Safety Protocols: Any safety measures or precautions to be taken.
Importance of Creating Work Orders
Work orders play a pivotal role in ensuring the smooth running of operations, be it in manufacturing, IT, or any other sector. They:
Facilitate Clear Communication: By providing detailed instructions and expectations, work orders eliminate ambiguity and ensure that tasks are executed correctly.
Enhance Accountability: With a documented trail of who authorized and who completed a task, there’s clear accountability.
Improve Efficiency: Structured work orders help in prioritizing tasks, allocating resources effectively, and reducing downtime.
Provide Data for Analysis: Completed work orders offer insights into operational efficiencies, recurring issues, and areas of improvement.
Comparison Between a Work Order and Work Request
While both terms are sometimes used interchangeably, there’s a subtle difference:
Work Request: Typically, a preliminary document or communication indicating that a task or maintenance activity needs attention. It’s often submitted by someone who identifies a problem but may not have the authority or expertise to address it.
Work Order: A formal authorization for the maintenance team to perform a specific task. It’s generated after evaluating the validity and priority of a work request.
In essence, a work request is the initiation, and the work order is the action.
Steps Involved in Creating a Perfect Work Order
Identify the Task:Before any work order is generated, there’s a need or problem that prompts it. This could arise from routine inspections, equipment malfunctions, or even external customer requests. Key considerations are as follows,
Understand the urgency of the task. Is it a critical issue that can halt production or a minor one that can wait?
Gather preliminary data. For instance, if it’s a machine malfunction, what were the symptoms? Did it make a noise? Did it overheat?
Request the Work Order:Once a task is identified, a formal work request is submitted. This acts as a preliminary document highlighting the problem or need. Key considerations are as follows,
Ensure clarity in the description. The more detailed the initial request, the easier it is to assess and prioritize.
Attach any relevant documentation or images that can provide additional context.
Approve and Create:Not all work requests translate into work orders. They need to be evaluated for validity, priority, and feasibility. Key considerations are as follows,
Assess the impact of the task on overall operations.
Consider the budgetary implications. Do we have the necessary resources, or will parts need to be ordered?
Ensure that the task aligns with regulatory and safety standards.
Assign the Work Order:Once approved, the work order needs a responsible party or team to execute it. Key considerations are as follows,
Match the complexity and nature of the task with the expertise of the technician or team.
Consider the workload of potential assignees. Overburdening can lead to mistakes and oversights.
Execute and Document:The assigned personnel carries out the task, ensuring that it’s completed to the set standards. Key considerations are as follows,
Follow safety protocols rigorously.
Document the process meticulously, noting down any challenges faced, tools used, parts replaced, and the time taken.
Capture before and after images if relevant, especially for tasks that have visual outcomes.
Review and Analyze:Post-completion, it’s essential to review the work order to glean insights and feedback. Key considerations are as follows,
Assess if the task was completed within the stipulated time frame.
Analyze any deviations from the expected outcome. Were there unforeseen challenges? Were additional resources required?
Use this analysis for continuous improvement. What went well? What can be done better next time?
Benefits of Using Work Order Management Software
Modern Work Order Management Softwareoffers a plethora of advantages:
Automation: Automatically schedule and assign tasks based on preset criteria.
Real-time Tracking: Monitor the progress of tasks in real-time.
Data Analytics: Gain insights from historical data to predict future maintenance needs and trends.
Resource Optimization: Efficiently allocate manpower and resources.
Enhanced Communication: Facilitate better communication between teams and departments.
Work Order Software vs. Pen and Paper
While traditional pen and paper methods have their charm, they are prone to errors, misplacements, and lack real-time tracking. In contrast, work order software offers digital accuracy, instant updates, and cloud storage, ensuring data is safe and accessible.
Work Order Software vs. Whiteboards
Whiteboards, though visual, are static and can become cluttered. Changes require manual updates, and there’s a risk of data being erased. Work order software, on the other hand, offers dynamic updates, scalability, and the ability to handle complex tasks with ease.
Work Order Software vs. Excel Spreadsheets
Excel spreadsheets are a step up from pen and paper but lack the automation and real-time capabilities of dedicated work order software. While spreadsheets can store data, they don’t offer the intuitive interfaces, instant notifications, or mobile capabilities that modern software provides.
Bottom Line
In today’s fast-paced world, efficiency and accuracy are paramount. Adopting a digital approach to work order management not only streamlines operations but also provides valuable insights, leading to continuous improvement and growth. Whether you’re a small business or a large enterprise, there’s a work order solution tailored to your needs, ready to propel you into the future of maintenance management.

Understanding MRP (Material Requirements Planning) Methodology: A Comprehensive Guide
In the realm of modern manufacturing and supply chain management, efficiency, accuracy, and timeliness are paramount. Material Requirements Planning (MRP) methodology stands as a cornerstone in achieving these objectives, facilitating seamless operations by ensuring the right materials are available at the right time in the right quantities. This comprehensive guide aims to delve into the intricacies of MRP, shedding light on its principles, benefits, implementation, and best practices.
What is Material Requirements Planning (MRP)?
At its core, MRP is a systematic approach to inventory management and production scheduling. It involves the use of computer-based systems to calculate the materials needed for production based on demand forecasts, existing inventory levels, lead times, and production schedules. By analyzing these factors, MRP helps manufacturers plan their material purchases and production activities more effectively, minimizing stockouts, reducing excess inventory, and optimizing resource utilization.
The Key Components of MRP:
1.Bill of Materials (BOM):A detailed list of all the components and sub-components required to manufacture a finished product. The BOM serves as the foundation for MRP, providing the necessary information about the materials, quantities, and relationships between components.
2.Master Production Schedule (MPS):A timetable that specifies the quantity and timing of production for each finished product. The MPS serves as the input to the MRP system, guiding the calculation of material requirements based on production needs.
3.Inventory Status:Information about the current inventory levels of raw materials, work-in-progress (WIP), and finished goods. This data is crucial for determining the materials needed to fulfill production orders while maintaining optimal inventory levels.
4.Lead Times:The time required to procure materials from suppliers, manufacture components, and assemble finished products. Lead times play a critical role in MRP calculations, helping to ensure that materials are available when needed to meet production deadlines.
Benefits of MRP:
1.Improved Inventory Management:By accurately forecasting material requirements and scheduling production activities, MRP helps companies minimize excess inventory and reduce carrying costs.
2.Enhanced Production Planning:MRP enables manufacturers to optimize production schedules, allocate resources efficiently, and meet customer demand more effectively.
3.Reduced Stockouts and Delays:By ensuring that the right materials are available at the right time, MRP helps prevent production delays and minimize the risk of stockouts, ensuring smooth operations and customer satisfaction.
4.Cost Savings:Through better inventory management, reduced waste, and improved resource utilization, MRP can lead to significant cost savings for businesses.
Implementing MRP:
Implementing MRP involves several steps:
1.Assessing Readiness:Evaluate your organization’s readiness for MRP implementation, including the availability of data, technology infrastructure, and organizational capabilities.
2.Selecting MRP Software:Choose an MRP software system that meets your organization’s needs, considering factors such as scalability, functionality, ease of use, and integration capabilities.
3.Data Preparation:Clean and organize your data, including BOMs, inventory records, production schedules, and lead time information, to ensure accuracy and consistency.
4.Training and Change Management:Provide comprehensive training to employees on how to use the MRP system effectively and communicate the benefits of the new approach to stakeholders.
5.Testing and Validation:Conduct thorough testing of the MRP system to ensure accuracy, reliability, and compatibility with existing processes before full-scale implementation.
6.Monitoring and Continuous Improvement:Regularly monitor MRP performance, analyze key metrics, and identify opportunities for optimization and refinement to ensure ongoing success.
Best Practices for MRP:
1.Maintain Accurate Data:Regularly update and maintain accurate data to ensure the reliability and effectiveness of the MRP system.
2.Collaborate with Suppliers:Establish collaborative relationships with suppliers to improve visibility into supply chain dynamics and reduce lead times.
3.Monitor Key Performance Indicators (KPIs):Track and analyze key performance indicators such as on-time delivery, inventory turnover, and production efficiency to measure the effectiveness of MRP.
4.Implement Demand Forecasting:Incorporate demand forecasting techniques to anticipate future demand trends and adjust production plans accordingly.
5.Review and Adjust Plans:Regularly review and adjust production plans based on changing market conditions, customer preferences, and business priorities.
Conclusion:
Material Requirements Planning (MRP) methodology serves as a cornerstone in modern manufacturing and supply chain management, enabling organizations to optimize inventory management, streamline production processes, and meet customer demand more effectively. By understanding the principles, benefits, and best practices of MRP, businesses can leverage this powerful tool to drive operational efficiency, reduce costs, and enhance competitiveness in today’s dynamic business environment.

Real time monitoring in computer integrated manufacturing
Definition of computational monitoring in real time
· Many structural, mechanical, and geotechnical systems, such as bridges, offshore and subsurface structures, power generation systems, rotating machinery, buildings, geotechnical foundations, boreholes, and mining excavations and tailings, and even cases involving living matter, require continuous information about performance and integrity of engineering systems in real time.
· The absence of timely, accurate, and consistent knowledge on manufacturing things (resources) during manufacturing execution is currently one of the most common difficulties that manufacturing firms encounter. Decision makers may make better-informed shop-floor decisions with real-time information visibility and traceability.
· The internet of manufacturing things (IoMT) as a real-time information capture and integration architecture to create a new paradigm by extending IoT principles to the manufacturing area. Manufacturing items such as operators, machines, pallets, and materials, among others, may be embedded with sensors and communicate with one another thanks to this architecture and its core components.
· A Real-time Manufacturing Information Integration Service (RTMIIS) has been designed to achieve seamless dual-way connectivity and interoperability among the enterprise layer, workshop floor layer, and machine layer, despite the challenges of processing a large amount of real-time data into useful information and exchanging it among heterogeneous application systems. Finally, a real-world situation was used to demonstrate the suggested IoMT’s proof-of-concept application.
Motivation for computational monitoring in real time
Novel materials are used in several engineering systems. Its long-term performance has yet to be established Continuous monitoring of the performance of the innovative materials and improved service time prediction are required for these systems. Transitioning to more cost-effective technologies may also need a reduction in safety margins. In this instance, safety necessitates more precise monitoring. Long-term monitoring observations may be used to update knowledge on system behaviour, which can then be incorporated through computational modelling to improve operational performance.
Rapid condition monitoring is necessary in extreme events to check the integrity of engineering systems and warn of impending failure or even disaster. In this case, computational monitoring allows for speedy response to quickly changing situations.
While the breakdown of an engineering structure or a structure in the Earth’s crust is generally an immediate occurrence that creates a critical point on the time axis, the processes that lead up to this critical event take time. Naturally, the monitoring is focused on these operations, the speed of which establishes the concept of’real time.’ We’ll suppose that these processes are defined by their characteristic times; the process’s characteristic time is the time it takes for the process to complete.
We also assume that the minimum typical time of the processes that lead to the system’s failure is known, and we’ll refer to it as the system’s characteristic time. As a result, monitoring in real time refers to a monitoring approach whose aggregated reaction time (the time required to acquire, analyse, and present the findings in a decision-making format) is less than the characteristic time of the system being monitored.
Many manufacturing organisations still face the following issues
1. To develop an overall data capture and integration architecture and solution to sense, process, and exchange real-time manufacturing data between the enterprise layer, workshop floor layer, and machine layer.
2. Determining how to quickly and efficiently implement IoT technology like RFID sensors for tracking and tracing manufactured items throughout the execution stage.
3. how to handle and integrate real-time production data in order to accomplish smooth dual processing enterprise layer, workshop floor layer, and machine layer communication and interoperability
Components of real-time computational monitoring
Computational monitoring is an interdisciplinary approach to monitoring. a study field that encompasses a variety of fundamental sciences, Mechanics, materials science, electronics, and other fields Computer science is the study of computers. The most important elements of a real-time system here are computational monitoring systems.
• Evaluation and non-destructive
• Processing of signal
• Monitoring data analysis and interpretations
• Actuators and sensors
• Computing at a high level
An overall real-time information capturing and integration architecture of the internet of manufacturing things (IoMT) is presented to provide a new paradigm by extending the IoT to the manufacturing field, taking into account the advantages of IoT and the requirements of real-time data driven optimal decision of the manufacturing execution system. Manufacturing objects, such as workers, equipment, pallets, and materials, may be integrated with sensors using this IoMT architecture. They can then engage with one another. As a result, the updated information and its state may be tracked and connected with a variety of business information systems (EISs). The proposed IoMT attempts to bridge the gap between enterprise management information systems and representative execution units like workstations and trolleys. It will make real-time data-driven optimum control and decision-making easier throughout industrial execution.
The Internet of Things (IoT) and its applications in the industrial industry
The Auto-ID centre popularised the Internet of Things concept. There have been a variety of definitions for the Internet of Things. According to Casagras (http://www.rfidglobal.eu/userfiles/documents/CASAGRAS26022009.pdf), the Internet of Things (IoT) is a global network architecture that connects physical and virtual items using data capture and communication capabilities. Existing and emerging Internet and network advancements are included in this infrastructure.
IoT is an integrated part of the Future Internet, according to CERP-IoT (Antoine de 2009), and can be defined as a dynamic global network infrastructure with self-configuring capabilities based on standard and interoperable communication protocols, where physical and virtual ‘things’ have identities, physical attributes, and virtual attributes.
Processing and integration of manufacturing data
When information is shared among heterogeneous application systems in real-life manufacturing organisations, difficulties in information integration may develop due to the many software applications employed in different enterprises.
As a result, manufacturing information standard models and schemas play a significant role in information exchange and integration across diverse corporate systems.
Siemens Energy & Automation, Inc. (2006) has created an interface that allows enterprise resource planning (ERP) and process control systems to communicate seamlessly. The challenges, trends, and difficulties for enterprise information interoperability are described by Panetto and Molin (2008). They claim that enterprise knowledge sharing, shared best practises, and open source/web-based applications make it possible to accomplish the idea of integrated enterprise, and hence networked enterprise implementation and interoperability. The ISA95 standard (ANSI/ISA 2000) was created with the goal of lowering the cost, risk, and mistakes involved with integrating enterprise and production control systems. The World Batch Forum (WBF) produced the business-to-manufacturing markup language (B2MML 2003) standard, which provides approved concepts and data. forms for exchanging information across management systems Anaya et al. (2010) present a unified model.
UEML (Enterprise Modeling Language) is a language for modelling businesses.
facilitating the usage of corporate information models represented in a variety of languages. To execute the information integration of heterogeneous information s0ystems, Zhang, Huang, and Qu (2011) use XML (extensible markup language) based schemas. For shop-floor work-in-progress (WIP) management, Fang, Huang, and Li (2013) describe an event-driven multi-agent ubiquitous manufacturing execution platform. Current industrial data integration models and methods, on the other hand, are primarily focused on heterogeneous corporate data systems. Because the crucial real-time data in IoMT originates straight from the basic events of Auto-ID devices, how do you develop a manufacturing information processing and integration approach that works across the enterprise layer, workshop floor layer, and cloud layer?
However, the overall integration architecture, real-time manufacturing data processing solution, and exchange standard among enterprise layer, workshop floor layer, and machine layer should be further designed based on the IoT infrastructure to make real-time production monitoring and control of the entire enterprise easy to deploy and use. Furthermore, the manufacturing information integration described above is already being utilised to deal with information sharing among third-party EISs; however, little thought has been given to how to seamlessly integrate and share real-time and multisource manufacturing data with third-party EISs. As a result, this study proposes and designs an overall real-time information capture and integration architecture for IoMT to solve the new problems.
IoMT’s overall architecture
With improved planning, scheduling, and control decisions, real-time traceability and visibility of manufacturing items plays a crucial role in increasing shop-floor performance. The goal of this study is to adapt the IoT idea to the manufacturing area and create a referenced real-time data collection and integration architecture for manufacturing companies. By referring to IoT infrastructure, an overall real-time data capturing and analysis. Real-time tracking and tracing of each manufacturing object (resource) is possible with this architecture. The entire production execution process may then be observed in real time. Sensor networks are used to monitor dynamical characteristics such as the environment (temperature, pressure, humidity, and so on), movement (velocity, acceleration, shock, and so on), and the real-time state of manufactured objects. It will give supervisors real-time data to execute optimal control and decision-making in a production execution system.
From the bottom to the top, the proposed IoMT consists of four components: configuration of smart manufacturing items, primitive event detection and capturing, manufacturing data processing, and application services.
Smart manufacturing object configuration
Smart manufacturing item configuration is responsible for increasing the sensing capabilities of all types of manufacturing objects (resources). The physical manufacturing resources are equipped with Auto-ID devices to reach a specific level of intelligence, which makes smart manufacturing things “smart.” In this IoMT framework, auto-ID techniques like RFID will be used to manufacturing resources like machines and production lines to create smart manufacturing objects that can detect the real-time state of manufacturing things including operators, materials, locations, and WIP items.
Sensing and recording of primitive events
The real-time primitive event of the sensors fitted to the manufacturing resources may be sensed and collected throughout the production process based on the setup of the smart manufacturing devices. A general technique is shown in Figure 2. The basic event can be perceived by the registered sensor when a manufactured object approaches a sensing region. The sensor can gather and transfer data from incoming manufacturing objects to the IoMT using the communication protocol and relationships in the registry. An RFID reader situated at a machine, for example, may detect and collect the electronic product code (EPC) of an operator wearing an RFID tag.
Data processing in manufacturing
A large quantity of real-time data collected by Auto-ID devices cannot be used directly in higher-level EISs. The data processing component in manufacturing is utilised to process the insignificant data into meaningful manufacturing information. Figure 3 illustrates a simple example of data processing. Take RFID technologies as an example: in sensing and capturing stage, the EPC of each tag attached to the manufacturing things is sensed and captured. However, this captured data is of no use for manufacturing system. Data processing is responsible for establishing the mapping relation and mechanism.
Conclusion
We’ve built the fundamentals for real-time computational monitoring. The computational monitoring has been defined.as a hybrid monitoring strategy that combines continuous measurement with real-time interpretation and forecasting Computational monitoring, in our opinion, is the next stage in the creation of intelligent engineering systems that can monitor their operating conditions, foresee faults, and govern their performance.
We’ve shown that standard monitoring approaches in several sectors of engineering share basic characteristics and face similar obstacles when it comes to incorporating data from various sources measurement. We also looked at the measurement methodologies and computational models that may be used to monitor diverse engineering systems in real time. The examination is brought to a close with examples from geotechnical engineering.
We anticipate that this study will spark discussion and cross-fertilization between monitoring approaches being developed in many fields of engineering, assisting in the resolution of computational monitoring difficulties, some of which are listed below.
· The essential features of the monitored system, such as stiffness, energy dissipation, and so on, are altered when damage accumulates. The challenge is to guarantee that the interpretation models are constantly and often adjusted in real time to adapt to system changes. This is especially significant for data collecting based on vibration, acoustic emission, and electromagnetic emission with model-based analysis.
• A key difficulty for computational monitoring systems is the design of the needed measurement system and sensor networks prior to deployment.The interpretation models must be able to react to changes in the measurement system, such as sensor failures at random.
• Another problem is the creation of correlation models between signal-based and model-based interpretation approaches. These models are required to guarantee that effective monitoring processes are in place.

title: Optimal Use of WIP Limits. Why is WIP Important? | by Michael Ryan | Medium
author: Michael Ryan
content:
Optimal Use of WIP Limits
Why is WIP Important?
Work-In-progress (WIP)is a concept that originated in the Lean manufacturing movement. In both a financial and operational sense WIP is considered a form of waste: work that has been done and paid for but is providing no benefit to the customer or the company.
WIP is an even more insidious problem in a software development context. In addition to financial and operational complications WIP imposes an additional tax on a software engineering team in the form of increased complexity and cognitive load.
WIP in Manufacturing
The ideal process in both manufacturing and software is often single-piece flow. In single-piece flow once work begins it continues without interruption until value is delivered to a customer. WIP is reduced to its theoretical minimal level with single-piece flow.
On the other hand, consider what happens in the absence of single-piece flow. Some value-adding work has been done on a product — but then work has to stop for a while before it continues and the product is finished. Maybe required materials are not present and the product must be stored until those materials arrive. Perhaps the product needs to be moved to another location before value-adding work can begin again — the time and expense involved in moving the product is a form of waste.
Partially finished items need to be kept track of, moved and stored until they can be completed and delivered to customers. The extra effort to do this provides no value to the customer or the company and is wasteful.
WIP in Software Development
The issues with partially finished work are similar in software development. In this context WIP is source code or other resources that have been created but are not yet in production producing value for users.
In most cases WIP takes the form of completed code that is not yet in production. It can be code on an engineer’s laptop that is not committed to a repository, code committed to a repository but not yet in a DevOps pipeline, or code in a DevOps pipeline waiting to be deployed. Either way it is waste: something that time and money has been spent on that is not producing value for the customer.
A software development team must spend precious cognitive bandwidth managing WIP. This takes effort and reduces the amount of time and energy that can be spent delivering features that provide value to the customer. In software development, as in manufacturing, it is very important to keep WIP at a minimum.
Cognitive load is a concept introduced in 1988 by psychologist John Sweller and recently made more popular by the book Team Topologies: Organizing Business and Technology Teams for Fast Flow by Matthew Skepton and Manuel Pais.
In software engineering there are three main ways cognitive load or mental capacity can be spent:
1) needless tasks that provide limited value such as manual deployments or paperwork,
2) well-known foundational elements of the current task like knowledge of a particular programming language or commonly used libraries, or
3) higher level “value add” thinking about architectural concerns or code-level tactical decisions like API design.
A team’s capacity to handle cognitive load is very limited. Great care must be taken to ensure the most time is spent on higher level “value add” thinking.
A high amount of WIP often means engineers are forced to work on more than one item at a time. Often a great many items at the same time. Paying attention to all these tasks increases the cognitive load on both individuals and the overall team while increasing the complexity of the tasks the team must handle. Excessive WIP can cause the performance and morale of a team to deteriorate badly.
On the other hand, low WIP implies each engineer can focus on just a few ( or ideally, one) thing at a time. The ideal state is when an engineer begins a task they have everything needed to complete that task and can work uninterrupted until that task is completed. There is often a small pause until that code passes code review, at which point it enters a build pipeline and again continues without interruption until it is released into production.
This seamless and constant flow of code reduces cognitive load on individuals and the overall team. Limiting WIP shortens the lead time for new features, reduces context switching, and allows engineers to concentrate resources and attention on the most important tasks. When engineers focus on only one thing at a time they are more productive and generally more satisfied with their work. They are more likely to stay with you.
What happens if automated testing and deployment of code changes is not in place? Then that code needs to be stored somewhere (often long running release branches) while waiting for approval. The team needs to keep track of what features are in what branch and be aware of any interactions between branches. In practice, there are often quite a few interactions between long running branches which makes testing difficult. The context switching involved in this approach imposes a high cognitive load on a team and greatly reduces their capacity to provide value to the customer and company.
The Wrong Branching Model Can Increase WIP
Gitflow vs Trunk-based Development
Many software engineering teams use long-running release branches, sometimes multiple release branches. In this approach releases are infrequent and the idea is to work on multiple features at once and have them scheduled for multiple release dates.
There may be valid business reasons this approach is used, and if that is the case then not much can be done. However, most often long-running release branches are in place simply because a team does not know how to deliver more frequent, smaller releases.
By definition, each of these long-running release branches contains WIP. By definition each release branch is WIP. Engineers have to keep track of what features are in each release branch while also developing new features. This sort of structure creates distraction and requires frequent context switching. It can be very error-prone.
Using the right branching strategy is critical to minimizing WIP. Branching models like Gitflow (https://nvie.com/posts/a-successful-git-branching-model/) split the code base into several long running branches, each designated for a future release. The cognitive load on a team using Gitflow tends to be high. They have to remember what each branch is for, what features are included in each branch, and how code in each branch interacts with other branches. There are many checks as code winds its way to production.
Gitflow is the right tool for certain use cases, but the payment for all the protection it offers are very large, infrequent releases and large amounts of WIP.
Gitflow: image by Vincent Driessen Trunk-based Development: image by Toptal
To reduce WIP (and increase deployment frequency/decrease deployment size), take a look at Trunk-based development (https://trunkbaseddevelopment.com/). Trunk-based development is a practice where developers merge small, frequent updates to a core main branch. Trunk-based development has strong support in the DevOps community as it streamlines merging, reduces WIP and reduces cognitive load.
How WIP Limits are Used
Many teams try to use WIP Limits as a way of reducing WIP and the waste and high cognitive load a high level of WIP places on a team. By focusing on an increasingly smaller number of tasks (the theoretical ideal WIP Limit is 1), WIP Limits are used to reduce rework and duplicative efforts, eliminate the context switching that comes with juggling multiple tasks, cut down on unnecessary meetings, improve communications and eliminate handoffs between teams or parts of teams.
What is a WIP Limit?
A WIP Limit is simply a limit on the number of unfinished tasks an engineer or team can work on at the same time. The optimal WIP limit is 1 — meaning an engineer works on only one task until that task is completed. Once the task is completed the engineer switches to the next task. The goal is to minimize (and ultimately prevent) multitasking and the context switching that happens each time an engineer stops working on one task and picks up another.
In many cases the rule is that if a WIP Limit is reached engineers perform non-coding tasks like code reviews, training, etc.
Reducing WIP to a bare minimum is an important goal in any DevOps or other workflow transformation. However, WIP Limits need to be used very carefully or they can backfire. This article provides a quick background on the concept WIP Limits as well as advice on how to best use WIP Limits.
As discussed, the optimal WIP Limit is one. In an ideal workflow, an engineer would work on one item until it is completed and passed off to an automated CI/CD pipeline that would then test and deploy that code. The engineer would then immediately begin work on the next item with no delay. In this scenario the engineer begins the task with everything needed to complete their task without interruption (the exception often being a little time spent waiting for code reviews).
Using WIP Limits for a Scrum Team
The illustration below shows a simple and hypothetical development team scrum board. Stories in the left column are not started, the middle column contains stories that are in progress, and finally the column on the right where completed stories are placed.
Example of team WIP limit of 4 tasks worked on at once.
WIP Limits deal with items in the “In Progress” column with the goal of reducing the number of tasks being simultaneously worked. On some teams WIP Limits apply to the entire team, while other teams apply WIP Limits to each individual. In either case the objective is to reduce the amount of work-in-progress and all the negative effects discussed above.
Where WIP Limits Work — and Where They Don’t
WIP Limits are often triggered when the entire engineering work stream is not set up for optimal flow. The typical symptom of non-optimal flow is when work on a story is partially completed, but then work has to stop while the engineer waits for clarification on requirements, waits for some approval to proceed further, or has to drop their work to focus on an important production defect.
If there is a WIP Limit of 1 then that blocked engineer is idle — they can’t work on anything else until the blockage is cleared. Idle engineers are obviously wasteful and few teams in this situation end up using WIP Limits for long, even if the idle time is used for training or other productive tasks.
An increase in idle engineers often ends up being the fatal flaw in using WIP Limits to spur process improvements. Idle engineers are usually only tolerated if:
A company is willing to let engineers be idle for possibly lengthy periods of time until the workflow is improved to the point where WIP Limits are not triggered.
The engineering team using WIP Limits controls the parts of the process that need improvement. If the delays triggering a WIP Limit are the result of another department (possibly QA or Operations) then the fact your team has reached a WIP Limit just may not matter to them. It’s possible these other groups might not be motivated to improve their pieces of the process so your team’s WIP Limits are not triggered.
Despite what anyone might say, most companies are not going to tolerate idle engineers for long. When the head of engineering complains their engineers are idle due to WIP Limits triggered because testing is not automated, the first question the group VP will ask is “Why can’t the engineers work on something else while they wait?” Be careful how you answer this question.
Arguing that WIP Limits are good because they reduce cognitive load and stress might not play well with stakeholders. One can always reduce cognitive load and stress simply by being idle. Instead the goal is to accomplish quite a bit while keeping cognitive load and stress in check. You don’t want to be on the wrong side of this argument.
Leading a Transformation
If you are leading an agile or devops transformation (or the second, third or fourth attempt at a transformation) you need to be aware of organizational history, internal politics and manage how your team presents itself across the company. If past transformations have failed or only been partially successful the organization might be jaded on the prospect of any improvement. There is likely a long backlog of engineering work the business would have liked to be completed long ago.
Stakeholders want engineers working to reduce that backlog. When stakeholders learn WIP Limits are reducing the amount of time engineers spend coding (even if only temporarily), precious political capital will need to be spent to keep them supporting the transformation.
Why incur that expense? You’ll need that political capital later, maybe if your team falls behind schedule or the first time you release a serious defect to production. Nothing ever goes as smoothly as you think it will.
We have found it more effective and less politically risky to challenge a team to improve DORA devops metrics instead of implementing WIP Limits. Focusing on improving Deployment Frequency coupled with Change Failure Rate is often a good place to start. If your team is currently deploying once per month, challenge them to deploy every two weeks, then weekly, then at will. And do that without increasing the number of defects found in production.
From the DORA 2021 Report:
Improving DORA metrics is a tangible task the team can focus on immediately. It will provide tangible benefits to the company. Tools like Value-Stream Mapping can be used to eliminate waste in any process. Remember, optimized processes minimize WIP. Accomplish just this and you’ll be making a substantial contribution to the good of the company.
The exception to this rule is if your team does not control the entire process. Maybe they are assigned to help another team by working on backlog items and they don’t have any control or input into Deployment Frequency. In this case WIP Limits might be helpful, at least as a tool to help other teams understand they need to improve their processes.
The Canary in the Coal Mine
WIP Limits do have one great advantage. A triggered WIP Limit is often the first indication a high performing engineering team is beginning to backslide. If engineers start hitting WIP limits it means your DORA metrics are soon to decline and you have a problem to solve. A good approach is to set a WIP Limit just above what the normal WIP level is. In this sense WIP Limits are like the proverbial canary in the coal mine — an early warning system.
To summarize, if you set a WIP Limit before flow is optimized you are bound to have engineers spend substantial time on non-engineering tasks. No one likes that. Engineers don’t like that and your business stakeholders surely won’t like that.
You can argue the slack time produced by WIP Limits will be spent on other important tasks like training. That may be true but we think this is a bad way to manage important tasks. Your team will never know when the WIP Limit will be triggered and when they can spend time training, or when WIP will drop under the WIP Limit and they have to get back to engineering work. This seems like a haphazard approach to something like training, which is an important part of your team’s professional development.
Building Software that Thrives on Change
In Kenzan’s experience engineering organizations can be broken down into three groups:
Base-levelengineering organizations employ many manual processes. Performance declines rapidly under a limited amount of change or load. Their capacity for improvement is small and they can only recover to baseline performance with extreme difficulty.
Effectiveengineering organizations produce good quality software while enduring a moderate amount of change or load. If stress exceeds a certain threshold performance rapidly declines. These organizations use some automated processes while still depending on manual work for important tasks. Their capacity for improvement is modest and they can recover to baseline performance with moderate difficulty.
Eliteengineering organizations grow stronger the more change or load is applied to them, in the same way the human body grows stronger through rigorous exercise. They actively seek to learn from mistakes and incorporate those learnings into future work, often embracing cloud infrastructure and cloud-native architectures. These organizations depend heavily on automation to increase quality while reducing cognitive load on teams and individuals. Their capacity for improvement is great and under stress they can recover to baseline performance with relative ease.
Getting Agile and DevOps transformations right is critical to becoming an elite engineering organization. If you’d like to discuss the concepts included in this article, please reach out to the author at mryan@kenzan.com.
Michael Ryan is Managing Principal Consultant and Head of Architecture at Kenzan.
