title: The QA Process: A beginner’s guide to the main stages, steps and tools of Quality Assurance | by Careerist | Medium
author: Careerist
content:
The QA Process: A beginner’s guide to the main stages, steps and tools of Quality Assurance
When you’re thinking about becoming a tester, and you’re reading about the topic, you can quickly become overwhelmed with all the concepts and terms associated with QA. There are so many terms in the QA process that don’t mean anything to you, like ‘black box’, ‘white box’, ‘unit tests’, ‘regression tests’, ‘manual’ and ‘automated’ testing, ‘BrowserStack’, and ‘Jira’…
It all sounds so complicated! Plus, you probably think that it’ll take you years to learn all of this stuff and to become a successful QA engineer!
Well, we won’t lie to you and say that becoming a QA engineer is simple and quick, because becoming a tester is going to require effort. But believe us when we say, it is not that hard to actually become a QA engineer. With adequate guidance and training you can learn pretty fast. You just need to know where to start.
This article will help you to understand the QA process, including, the testing steps, and what tools are generally used by engineers. After reading this article you will know:
What is the difference between quality assurance and quality control?
What are the main stages in the QA process?
What is the difference between manual and automated testing?
What do the different ‘test types’ mean?
Which tools help to optimize the entire QA process?
What is the QA process and how is it different from quality control?
QA, or quality assurance, in software development is a process that checks and prevents any issues occurring across the whole project. This also includes project management, as various individuals need to be managed when performing QA tests. And finally, QA also guarantees that a company delivers a product or software to market that has the best possible user experience.
Quality control (QC), on the other hand, focuses on testing the final product and identifying issues and eliminating them, before the product goes on the market.
Having a functioning QA process ensures that all of the team members, who are working on a particular project, work more effectively together and in doing so the development time will shorten, and thus costs will be lower.
Of course, the QA testing process varies slightly in different companies. But in general, its stages are the same.
Now you know more about the QA process let’s take a look at the main stages within the QA process.
What are the main stages in the QA process?
Review of requirements
Nowadays, quality assurance starts very early in the software development lifecycle – right in the ‘requirement analysis’ stage. QA professionals must review the requirements of the product before starting work, so that they can be clear on what needs to be done. Checking the requirements also means that the testing will be consistent, complete, executable, and that the project is actually testable.
Planning phase
After testers have understood the requirements, they can start developing a test strategy and begin the test planning phase. At this stage, they define the scope of the work, the budget, they decide which approach to take at each stage of the software’s development, they’ll also decide what types of testing will be needed, and finally, which tools will be used during the actual testing.
Developing test cases
With a plan in hand, it is time to design test cases, create checklists, prepare the environment for test execution, and create automated testing scenarios.
Test execution
At this point, everything is prepared for finding bugs and issues. The QA team starts to execute different types of tests, and testers start to report any and all of the discovered bugs.
Verifying fixes
Once the development team fixes an issue, QA professionals retest the functionality of the product, and perform regression testing to ensure that the software still works correctly after all of the changes have been made.
Test cycle closure
Once all of the fixes have been changed, and all planned tests have been executed, it is time to prepare the test closure document. This document is a summary of all the tests performed during the software development life cycle.
What tests are used in the QA process, and what approaches are considered?
Now that you understand what the QA process looks like, let’s now talk about all the different test types that can be used in software testing. Yes, there are a lot of them, but don’t worry, you’ll soon be able to navigate between them.
Functional and non-functional tests
There are two main tests categories, these are, functional and non-functional tests.
In functional testing, QA engineers check to see whether the product behaves as required. In other words, they verify if the actual output is matching the expected result.
In non-functional testing, the QA engineer checks how the product performs in different conditions. They will change the environments to see what happens, for example, load, security, stress, and usability tests.
Knowledge of the source code
If testers know the source code before testing begins, then QA engineers use the ‘white box’ testing type. On the other hand, if QA engineers do not know the source code they are dealing with, the ‘black box’ testing type is used. This is when testers only evaluate input and output in an application.
On a different note, ‘grey box’ testing is a combination of both of these approaches, and testers use this type of testing when they have limited information about the internal structure of the system.
A phase of software development
This is when tests are divided up into; unit testing, module testing, integration testing, system testing, and user acceptance testing, based on where developers are in the software development cycle.
Here are a couple more testing types that you may come across:
Smoke tests are designed to check the basic functionality of an application. They are quick to perform, and with their help, testers can ensure that the main features of the system are working correctly.
Regression tests help to check if an application is working as it is supposed to be working after some changes, such as bug fixes, are done.
Load tests are needed to determine an application’s behavior both under average and peak load conditions.
Cross-browser/cross-platform testing helps to analyze the application’s behavior in different browser/platform environments.
Of course, these are not all of the testing types used in the QA test process. But knowing the basic categories will help you to understand the topic better.
Approaches to executing tests
Some tests are performed by humans and this is known as manual testing. In manual testing, testers actually execute test cases and generate test reports themselves.
On the other hand, you have tests that are performed by computers, this is more commonly known as automation. Test automation engineers are responsible for creating and writing test codes that simulate user experiences, that can be repeated over and over again, to check the software in question for bugs.
Both of these approaches have pros and cons, and when used together they yield good results.
Here are some things about manual testing to consider. Manual testing is more suited for small test projects, and manual tests typically pick up issues that would be missed in an automated test. And finally, manual testing doesn’t require advanced knowledge of scripting languages and is reasonably easy to learn.
On the flip side, manual testing is time-consuming if testers are working on a big project, and you can never exclude the possibility of human error.
Similarly, automation has many positives, it can be used repeatedly, time and time again. Plus, it’s good for large projects. But, on the downside, it doesn’t quite have the human touch and can miss errors that are beyond the scope of its code.
QA professionals have to decide between manual and automated testing for each project.
Tools
Now that we know what the QA process is and what types of tests and approaches exist, let’s talk about what tools testers use when they’re completing their work. A testing tool is anything that supports test activities.
There are plenty of tools on the market, and nobody expects a beginner to know them all. But it’s a good idea to be familiar with the most popular tools, like ‘Selenium’, ‘Jira’, and ‘BrowserStack’.
‘Selenium’ is the most popular testing tool. It does not need advanced scripting knowledge and is user friendly for beginners.
‘Jira’ is a bug and issue tracking tool. It is also used for project management.
‘BrowserStack’ enables developers to test their applications across different browsers, devices, and operating systems.
Conclusion
No matter which approach or method a company uses, the final goal is always the same – to deliver the best possible product to customers.
Well established QA processes help to reduce costs, improve the overall quality of software, and bring about a better user experience.

Online Payment Gateway Integration: A Thorough Guide
Selecting a suitable payment gateway is critical to enhancing the customer shopping experience. E-commerce entities must effortlessly acceptdiverse payment methodsto thrive. Nonetheless, the integration of payment gateways entails intricate procedures.
Boasting over nine years in custom software development,Softermiideeply understands the technical demands for integrating payment gateways into e-commerce platforms. Our proficiency equips us to impart comprehensive knowledge to businesses about enabling their customers’ favored payment methods. This article delves into gateway solutions’ varied types and attributes and examines the associated integration costs.
Varieties of Payment Gateways
Payment gatewaysact as digital sentinels for financial transactions. They safeguard the transfer of funds from the buyer’s bank to the seller’s during online purchases. The choice of a payment gateway hinges on your enterprise’s needs, technical prowess, and the customer experience you wish to offer.
Hosted Payment Gateways
These gateways reroute customers from a site to the gateway’s platform for transaction completion, returning them to the original site post-transaction.
They are easy to implement and oversee, as the processor manages security and PCI compliance. However, this redirection might interrupt the user experience, potentially leading to abandoned carts.
Integrated Payment Gateways
These gateways meld seamlessly with e-commerce sites using APIs, allowing in-site transaction processing.
Integrated gateways enhance user experience and brand consistency but demand technical know-how for setup and maintenance. Some security and PCI compliance responsibilities also fall on the business.
Self-hosted Payment Gateways
Companies collect payment information in this model and forward it to the gateway’s URL.
Self-hosted gateways offer extensive customization and control over user interactions. However, directly handling customer data entails greater security and compliance obligations.
Local Bank Integration
Shoppers are redirected to their bank’s website for payment and returned to the original site.
This method is often viewed as more trustworthy due to familiar bank interfaces. However, like hosted gateways, redirection might dissuade some customers.
Direct Post Method
Payment processing occurs on the business’s site while the gateway’s servers execute the transaction. This shift is typically imperceptible to the user.
This type shares security responsibilities between the business’s site and the payment processor. Still, some security duties remain with the business.
Mobile Payment Gateways
These are specifically designed for mobile applications optimized for smooth mobile transactions.
This approach facilitates quicker mobile checkouts and leverages the expanding mobile commerce sector. However, certain gateways might necessitate additional integrations or configurations for mobile platforms.
Essential Attributes of Payment Gateways
A proficient payment gateway transcends mere transaction facilitation. It should be secure, user-friendly, adaptable, and reliable. When seeking an optimal gateway, businesses should consider these attributes:
Robust Security and Fraud Prevention
Payment gateways should employ SSL encryption and tokenization and offer fraud detection mechanisms like address verification systems (AVS) and card verification value (CVV) checks.
Effortless Integration
Gateway APIs should integrate smoothly with diverse platforms, be compatible with key shopping carts and e-commerce systems, and provide SDKs for developer use.
User-Oriented Design
Gateways must be intuitively designed, with rapid checkout options, and mobile optimization is increasingly advantageous.
Consistent Customer Support
Around-the-clock assistance should be accessible via phone, chat, and email.
Dynamic Reporting Capabilities
Real-time analytics and tailored reporting features provide valuable sales and performance insights.
Recurring Billing Feature
Gateways should support automated recurring payments and offer flexible billing schedules for businesses with subscription models.
Diverse Payment Methods
Gateways should accept major credit and debit cards, be compatible with popular digital wallets, and integrate with bank transfers and cryptocurrencies.
Optimal Uptime and Dependability
Systems should consistently be operational, minimizing downtime and swiftly processing transactions.
Selecting an Appropriate Payment Gateway
Consider factors impacting customer abandonment, sales, and trust when choosing a gateway. Here are some aspects to contemplate:
Security Standards
Verify the gateway’s adherence to PCI DSS requirements and its fraud protection capabilities.
Cost Analysis
Examine the gateway’s pricing structure, including transaction fees, monthly charges, setup costs, and potential hidden fees.
Payment Method Support
Choose a gateway supporting various payment methods like credit/debit cards and e-wallets.
Global and Multi-Currency Support
Ensure the gateway supports currency conversion and localized payment options for different regions or countries for international reach.
Reputation and Feedback
Gather insights from other businesses about their experiences with potential gateways.
The Integration Process of Online Payment Gateways
Integrating a payment gateway is pivotal for businesses, facilitating secure transactions and enhancing the purchasing process. Here’s an outline of the integration steps:
Project Scoping and Planning
Businesses should identify specific requirements, such as operational regions, accepted currencies, or transaction volumes. It informs the choice of a suitable payment gateway or developinga P2P payment application.
Integration Design
The focus then shifts to designing the payment process, ensuring an intuitive customer journey from shopping cart to payment confirmation. The design should facilitate a seamless checkout while the backend manages data processing and gateway communication.
Integration Implementation
After selecting a payment system, developers use the provided API for website integration, setting up the backend for transaction handling. It includes processing payment requests and responses. Front-end developers implement theUI/UX designson payment pages, ensuring functionality and user-friendliness.
Testing and Deployment
Engineers test transactions in the gateway’s sandbox environment before launching, confirming correct payment processing. User testing helps identify and resolve any issues. After addressing all concerns, the system transitions from the sandbox to live operation.
Ongoing Maintenance
Continuous updates and monitoring are vital to maintain the integration’s effectiveness and durability. Regular maintenance ensures the system stays abreast of the latest technologies and security protocols, safeguarding against vulnerabilities.
Documentation
Post-integration, creating comprehensive documentation of the process is crucial. It includes details from API specifics to maintenance strategies, ensuring continuity and adaptability for future needs.
When executed proficiently, the multifaceted nature of payment gateway integration can significantly benefit an e-commerce venture. Opt for a company with adedicated, experienced teamto provide customers with a secure and seamless experience.
Payment Gateway Integration Cost
Creating an online payment platform from scratch is optional, but hidden and indirect costs are often overlooked. To budget effectively and select a cost-efficient option, comprehend all factors influencing integration expenses. Let’s explore these factors.
Setup Charges
Some gateways impose a setup fee for service access. The amount varies based on brand reputation and feature offerings.
Subscription Fees
Providers may adopt a monthly or annual subscription model, either flat-rate or transaction volume-dependent.
Per-Transaction Fees
A common fee involves charges per transaction, usually a percentage of the transaction value, occasionally with an additional fixed rate.
Cross-Border Charges
For international customer sales, extra fees may apply for transactions in different currencies or from abroad.
Integration Costs
While major platforms may offer pre-built plugins for common CMS and e-commerce systems, bespoke integrations incur additional development costs.
Chargeback Penalties
In transaction disputes resulting in chargebacks, gateways may apply a fee to cover administrative costs and incentivize quality service.
Security Expenses
Investments in additional security measures like SSL certificates or advanced fraud protection incur separate costs, though crucial for safe payment processing.
Maintenance and Upgrades
Regular updates to the integration are necessary due to changes in gateway APIs or new security and feature standards. These periodic updates may entail costs.
Contract Termination Penalties
Contracts with certain providers might incur termination fees if they switch systems before the contract ends.
Extra Feature Costs
Services like advanced analytics, dedicated support, or enhanced fraud protection may attract additional charges.
Compliance Expenditures
Ensuring compliance with PCI DSS and other regulations might necessitate adjustments to your setup, leading to further costs.
Case Studies and Examples of Payment Gateway Integration
Examining successful payment gateway integrations showcases how they have revolutionized business operations and customer interactions. Here are some illustrative cases:
Walmart & PayPal
Walmart Marketplace aimed to empower smaller sellers on their platform, aspiring to elevate quality and expand payout options and platform innovations.
Solution
In 2019, Walmart integrated PayPal’s Hyperwallet for payouts, offering diverse payout methods and leveraging PayPal’s trustworthiness.
Outcome
Many new sellers opted for Hyperwallet, facilitating smooth operations and fostering understanding between customers and sellers. It also aligned with Walmart’s goal of nurturing a premium seller community.
Lyft & Stripe
Lyft drivers sought more frequent payouts than the traditional weekly schedule. The challenge was to provide payments at the drivers’ convenience without disruptions.
Solution
Lyft partnered with Stripe to create Express Pay, enabling drivers to choose their payout times, sometimes within hours after completing a ride.
Outcome
Within six months of the integration, over 40% of Lyft drivers had chosen Express Pay, significantly attracting more drivers to the platform.
Due South & Square
Due South aimed to incorporate smooth online payments in its online expansion strategy. Many solutions were either exclusively for online stores or required simplification for quick adoption.
Solution
In 2020, Due South launched an online store utilizing Square’s online payment gateway. They integrated their inventory information, ensuring online products reflected real-time stock levels to prevent overselling.
Outcome
Square’s solution ensured continuous business operations and boosted Due South’s online sales, demonstrating the importance of a well-integrated payment system.

Each project provided valuable insights into balancing user experience, business needs, and regulatory compliance. Payment integration is a key area of our expertise, simplifying commerce for innovative businesses across various sectors.
Concluding Thoughts
The choice of a payment gateway should align with your business’s immediate and future aspirations. Regardless of the selected gateway type, prioritize security, dependability, and user-friendliness. Achieving the right balance between operational demands, costs, and customer experience is crucial for maximizing benefits.

It lies between the enterprise level and tool level control system.

What is Enterprise resource planning (ERP) ? The ERP Software Guide
Meaning of Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP)
Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) is a comprehensive business management software that integrates and streamlines various core processes and functions across an entire organization.The aim is to enhance efficiency, facilitate data flow between different departments, and provide real-time insights for informed decision-making.ERP systemstypically cover a range of business areas, such as finance, human resources, supply chain management, manufacturing, procurement, and more.
The fundamental concept behind ERP is to replace disparate, often disconnected software applications with a unified platform. This integration allows for a centralized database that serves as a single source of truth, ensuring consistency in data and processes. ERP software automates routine tasks, standardize business processes, and enable the sharing of information across different departments. This holistic approach to business management enhances collaboration, reduces manual efforts, and contributes to the overall optimization of organizational workflows.
What is ERP Software:
ERP software refers to the application or suite of applications that organizations use to implement Enterprise Resource Planning. These software solutions are designed to automate and integrate business processes, allowing for the efficient flow of information across an entire enterprise. ERP software typically includes various modules, each catering to a specific functional area within an organization. Common modules encompass finance, human resources, inventory management, customer relationship management (CRM), procurement, and supply chain management.
ERP software provides a centralized platform where users from different departments can access, input, and utilize data. This promotes collaboration and ensures that everyone in the organization is working with consistent and up-to-date information. ERP systems are customizable to some extent, allowing organizations to tailor the software to their specific needs and industry requirements. The implementation ofERP softwareis a strategic decision for businesses aiming to improve operational efficiency, enhance decision-making, and stay competitive in a rapidly evolving business landscape.
Enterprise Resource Planning Vs Systems, Applications, and Products
ERP (Enterprise Resource Planning):
Definition: ERP refers to a category of software that integrates and manages key business processes across an organization. It includes modules for finance, human resources, supply chain management, manufacturing, and other critical functions.
Scope: ERP systems can be developed by various vendors, and they are not limited to a specific brand or product. Many companies offer ERP solutions, and each may have its strengths and weaknesses.
Examples: Besides SAP, other well-known ERP vendors include Oracle, Microsoft Dynamics, and Infor. Each of these vendors provides ERP solutions with unique features and functionalities.
SAP (Systems, Applications, and Products):
Definition: SAP is a specific ERP software vendor that provides a suite of software applications designed to support business processes such as financial accounting, supply chain management, human resources, and more.
Scope: While SAP is a major player in the ERP market, it is not the only one. SAP ERP solutions are widely used globally and are known for their robustness and versatility.
Examples: SAP offers various ERP solutions, such as SAP S/4HANA for large enterprises,SAP BusinessOne for small to medium-sized businesses, and industry-specific solutions like SAP ERP for Manufacturing or SAP ERP for Retail.
Types of ERP Software
Finance Module:
Manages financial transactions, accounting, and financial reporting.Includes functionalities such as accounts payable, accounts receivable, general ledger, and financial analysis.Streamlines financial processes to ensure accuracy and compliance.Facilitates real-time monitoring and analysis of the organization’s financial health.

Manages the end-to-end supply chain processes, including procurement, inventory management, order fulfillment, and logistics.Aims to optimize the flow of goods and information throughout thesupply chain.Enhances visibility and collaboration across the entire supply chain network.Improves efficiency by minimizing delays and reducing inventory carrying costs.

Focuses on production planning, scheduling, and shop floor control.Manages manufacturing processes, resource allocation, and production efficiency.Improves production agility through real-time data and analytics.Ensures quality control and adherence to manufacturing standards.

Evolution of ERP
Early Systems (1960s-1970s):
ERP has its roots in Materials Requirements Planning (MRP) systems that emerged in the 1960s. These early systems focused on managing inventory and production scheduling.MRP II (Manufacturing Resource Planning), which evolved in the 1970s, expanded the scope to include additional business functions like finance, human resources, and more.
Birth of ERP (1980s):
The term “Enterprise Resource Planning” was coined in the early 1980s as software developers recognized the need for integrated solutions that could address various business processes.Companies began developing ERP systems to provide a unified platform for managing different aspects of an organization.
SAP R/3 (1990s):
In the early 1990s, SAP introduced its R/3 system, a client-server architecture that marked a significant milestone in ERP history.R/3 integrated various business processes, offering modules for finance, human resources, supply chain, and more. SAP R/3 quickly became a leading ERP solution globally.
Expansion and Competition (Late 1990s-2000s):
The late 1990s and early 2000s witnessed the expansion of ERP systems into different industries beyond manufacturing.Other major ERP vendors, including Oracle and PeopleSoft, entered the market, intensifying competition and offering a variety of ERP solutions.
Cloud ERP (2010s-Present):
In the 2010s, there was a shift towards cloud-based ERP solutions.Cloud ERPoffered advantages like scalability, accessibility, and reduced infrastructure costs.Established ERP vendors and new players introduced cloud-based solutions to meet the evolving needs of businesses.
Integration of Emerging Technologies (2010s-Present):
The ERP landscape in recent years has seen the integration of emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, machine learning, and the Internet of Things (IoT).
These technologies enhance the functionality of ERP systems, providing advanced analytics, automation, and improved decision-making capabilities.
Focus on User Experience and Mobility:
Modern ERP systems emphasize user experience and mobility, with intuitive interfaces and mobile access to enable users to work from various devices and locations.
Industry-Specific Solutions:

title: Chart of Accounts Best Practice Tips - a Dynamics Consultant’s Perspective | by Cherub Robertson | Hitachi Solutions Braintrust | Medium
author: Cherub Robertson
content:
Chart of Accounts Best Practice Tips — a Dynamics Consultant’s Perspective
At the heart of ERP, a chart of accounts (COA) can be found branching out through the business. As part of an ERP implementation, the COA needs to be cleaned up and made extensible, preparing it for ease of use and growth with the business post new ERP implementation. COAs can be global in Dynamics or vary by legal entity, depending on the organization’s needs. It takes time and effort to come up with a well-thought out, well-designed COA.
A new COA requires mapping of old data from the legacy system to the new COA for data migration. Data validation after a new COA implementation can be quite cumbersome. In testing after COA modification, you may find changes or additions must be made for best fit to the business or for Dynamics-required setups. The COA has to be made to work for the business and the new ERP and, as the client becomes better versed in the new ERP, additional tweaks to the COA will likely be necessary.
Here are some best practice tips that can be used to facilitate the COA revision process:
1. Don’t wait!It is critical that the conversation with the client around COA revision start early. The COA revision should be as complete as it can be prior to the first load for initial Dynamics configuration. An overhaul of the COA post-ERP setup can be very time-consuming, requiring not only an update of the COA itself, but of Main Account-referencing Posting Profiles and other Dynamics configurations.
2. Get everyone involved. Encourage the finance contact(s) responsible for the COA overhaul on the client side to work closely with contacts from other parts of the business to make sure everyone’s needs are being heard and met. Consider the organizational structure/hierarchy. Do the financial dimensions (segments) capture all that is needed for separation of activity, or should the detail be captured in additional main accounts that are, perhaps, unique to various parts of the business?
3. How many digits?How many characters would the client like used for main account numbers in Dynamics? Between four and six are common lengths. Prior to import, verify all main accounts meet the decided-on length. Main account masking on the COA can be configured as a control to ensure newly created or changed main account numbers in Dynamics meet the necessary length and all characters are numeric. Alpha characters can be used in main account numbering and included in masking, too, but is not seen very often.
4. Account numbering. Overall COA numbering follows balance sheet and income statement presentation. The first digit of main accounts enables grouping of like, high-level sets of accounts and typically follows the below standard:
The second digit in a main account number is used to classify subsets of the primary groupings defined by the main account first digit. Here is an example of how you might see second digits employed in the assets grouping:
A digit might be selected to identify accounts possessing similar properties. For example, contra accounts might all end in the number “9” to make them stand out:
Remaining digits can be used to classify other traits or subsets of accounts if needed, along with at least one unique identifier to specifically pinpoint the subject account.
5. Extensibility. Main account numbering should allow for easy growth of the COA with the business while maintaining the order of accounts. Gaps between main account numbers should be part of planning the COA revision. Gap size appropriate for the business depends on the frequency of the addition of new accounts and COA changes. In the example below, a gap of 10 numbers has been left between main accounts to allow for the creation of future new accounts that may need to be inserted to retain the planned structure of the COA. In this example, an “in transit” bank account for a bank that already exists is being set up for use as a bridging account:
6. Beware of special characters. Main account names can usually be whatever the client needs them to be in Dynamics. When you get into the financial report builds however, you may encounter errors in the Report Designer due to disallowed special characters.
7. Legal entity override.You can take advantage of the option to prohibit use of main accounts in specified Dynamics legal entities without having to implement additional COA. Configuration can be done at the main account or via entity load.
8. Spell check. Prior to import, it is a good idea to perform one last check.
Summary
Overhaul of the COA is quite a task to take on, especially under the pressure and demands of a new ERP implementation. Helpful hints are good to have but a second set of eyes is invaluable. As the consultant and expert, perform a careful review of the COA presented by the client for use in Dynamics and meet/discuss until all looks good. You, of course, want the client to be pleased with the finished product so don’t be afraid to provide feedback and constructive criticism when needed. Little things, like spell check, are easily overlooked with tasks this big and the client will appreciate your help.

title: How the Chart of Accounts Can Help You and Why You Should Care | by Lianabel Oliver | Medium
author: Lianabel Oliver
content:
How the Chart of Accounts Can Help You and Why You Should Care
As an entrepreneur, you have probably not given much thought to your chart of accounts. You may not even know what a chart of accounts is or have even seen one for your business. After all, you delegated this task to your accountant or used the automated setup function of your accounting software application. However, the initial design of your chart of accounts is probably one of the most important decisions you will make during your system setup and the key to extracting financial information for decision-making and financial planning purposes, including taxes.
Thegeneral ledgeris the backbone of any accounting system and contains all the business transactions of your company expressed in monetary terms. It is structured according to the chart of accounts, which you define during the initial setup of your accounting system. Thechart of accountsgroups similar transactions into general or specific categories, which should reflect your business and how you want to collect and report financial information. The chart of accounts should also satisfy your own internal needs for information as well as legal and tax reporting requirements.
The chart of accounts follows a logical sequence, which reflects the way information is reported on the financial statements. In general, automated accounting systems such as Quicken, Sage or QuickBooks, among many others, will recommend a chart of accounts based on your business type (manufacturing, service, non-profit) or industry, and organize it by major accounting classifications: assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, and expenses.
You may be asking yourself: if an automated system does all the work, why bother to review or understand it? Isn’t that the reason I have an accountant to do the bookkeeping and tax filings? There are two good reasons why you should be involved in the setup of your chart of accounts. First, the suggested accounts provided by the application you are using may or may not be applicable to your business, resulting in unnecessary accounts. Second, the chart of accounts should reflect your business. No one knows your business better than you!
What are the consequences of a poorly configured chart of accounts? Mainly, rework, inefficiencies, and poor decision making due to inaccurate financial information. Your accountants or data entry personnel may get confused as to where to book a revenue or an expense item or record it inconsistently — one month in one account and the next month in another. They may require manual processes to extract and prepare the information you need to manage the business.
So, sit down with your accountant and review the chart of accounts. Add new accounts for information that you want to track, and eliminate accounts for information that you do not need. If your chart of accounts is too detailed, it may cause data entry errors and as a result, produce inaccurate financial information. Most accounting software applications will also allow you to track financial information that is not captured in your account structure. For example, would you like to see a profit and loss statement (P&L) by distribution channel, by product family, or by customer type? An accounting system that is properly configured will allow you to report this information.
If you have a system already up and running, do not despair. Most software applications allow you to change your chart of accounts with relative ease without destroying the historical data or losing the audit trail. The most important task is to sit down with your accountant, review your chart of accounts, and determine whether it is recording your business transactions according to your information needs. Make sure it is complete but keep it simple! Once you have defined what you really need, let your accountant worry about the details of the implementation.
A poorly configured accounting system can become a drag for your business. I have seen small, medium, and large companies run parallel accounting systems on spreadsheet applications because they cannot trust or use the information they receive. So, if your accounting system is not providing you with the information you need, remember — it all starts with the chart of accounts.

title: Payment Processing: How Does It Work? | by Chirag Dave | Medium
author: Chirag Dave
content:
As technology advances, cash is slowly becoming obsolete. Secure and convenient digital transactions are now the norm, even in brick-and-mortar stores. They boost customer satisfaction, enhance security and transparency in payments, and minimize risks like theft and counterfeit bills associated with cash.
With more businesses adopting digital tools, online transactions are poised for even greater popularity. Statista predicts the global value of digital payments to hit a staggering $14.79 trillion USD by 2027. Consequently, the demand for payment processing services is surging worldwide.
This article delves into payment processing, its key elements, and explores the pros and cons of integrating it into custom software solutions.
What is Payment Processing?
In our world of online and mobile payments, payment processing is the vital behind-the-scenes magic that enables secure money transfers. It handles everything from credit card transactions to mobile wallets, digital currencies, and more. While building and maintaining a standalone payment system is complex and regulated, integrating existing payment solutions into custom software is crucial for businesses of all sizes. This is especially true for the booming e-commerce market, projected to reach a whopping $8.1 trillion by 2026.
The Three Pillars of Digital Payments:
Digital Commerce:This covers online transactions through websites or apps, using methods like credit cards or PayPal. Think online shopping, where you browse and pay directly within the app or website.
Mobile POS (Point-of-Sale) Payments:Here, contactless payments reign supreme. Customers tap their smartphones (with mobile wallets) or devices with NFC chips (like smartwatches or fitness trackers) at terminals in stores, restaurants, and more.
Digital Remittances:This innovative method offers a secure and convenient way to send money internationally. Using mobile apps or websites, users can skip traditional banks and benefit from lower fees and exchange rates.
Key Components in Payment Processing
In our world of online and mobile payments, payment processing is the vital behind-the-scenes magic that enables secure money transfers. How Does Payment Processing Work?
When you make a digital purchase, a smooth process ensures the funds securely move from your account to the merchant’s. Here’s a simplified breakdown of the five key steps in this payment processing flow:
Step 1: Initiating the Payment
The customer interacts with the merchant’s point-of-sale (POS) system. This could involve swiping a card, using contactless payment (like a mobile wallet), or entering card details on an online checkout. The POS system then sends the payment amount and card information securely to the acquiring bank via a payment gateway.
Step 2: Reaching Out for Approval
The acquiring bank, representing the merchant, receives the payment details and reaches out to the customer’s issuing bank through the appropriate card network. This step essentially asks the issuing bank for permission to complete the transaction.
Step 3: Verification and Authorization
The issuing bank, representing the customer, verifies the received information — card number, CVV code, expiration date — and checks if sufficient funds are available. If everything is valid, the issuing bank sends an authorization code back to the acquiring bank using the same card network.
Step 4: Fund Authorization and Reserve
Upon transaction approval, the issuing bank sets aside the purchase amount from the customer’s account. This signifies the customer’s go-ahead for the payment, although the funds haven’t moved to the merchant’s account yet.
Step 5: Batching and Settlement
Approved transactions are grouped into batches. The merchant submits the daily batch of transactions with their authorization codes to the acquiring bank or payment processor. The acquirer then requests the authorized amounts from the issuing bank, triggering the transfer of funds from customers’ accounts to the merchant’s account. Payment processing fees are also deducted during this stage.
Importance of Payment Processing for Businesses
While paying digitally seems effortless for customers, it involves a complex technical process for businesses. However, the advantages are undeniable. Businesses that have embraced payment processing reap numerous benefits with every transaction. Here’s a glimpse into the advantages for both businesses and their customers:
Better Service and Customer Experience
Payment processing systems are game-changers for transaction speed. What used to take days can now be completed in seconds, thanks to these efficient tools. But their benefits go beyond speed. Payment processors also ensure the smooth completion of every electronic transaction, guaranteeing both accuracy and reliability.
This translates to a frictionless customer experience. Gone are the days of waiting for checks to clear or dealing with complex paperwork. With payment processing, a few taps or clicks on a device is all it takes to complete a purchase. An added bonus for customers? Simplified refunds and chargebacks, further enhancing convenience.
Enhanced Security
Handling sensitive customer data like credit cards is a top concern for businesses of all sizes. This is where payment processing shines. Reputable third-party processors or custom-built systems prioritize security by adhering to strict compliance standards like PCI certificates. These standards safeguard customer information from unauthorized access and data breaches.
Reliable payment processing systems go a step further by utilizing encrypted channels to shield transactions from fraud. Features like multi-factor authentication (MFA) add another layer of security, protecting both businesses and their customers during digital purchases.
Cost Reduction
Paper checks and cash transactions are cumbersome and time-consuming, requiring extra steps for both sending and receiving payments. Businesses, in particular, face a burden of additional costs: banking fees, secure disposal charges, and other expenses associated with outdated paper-based methods.
Payment processing systems offer a powerful solution. By integrating a secure system, businesses can significantly reduce these costs. Managing paper transactions often necessitates a larger accounting staff. However, with efficient payment processing, businesses can potentially minimize their accounting team to just one or two specialists. This translates to substantial cost savings for businesses of all sizes.
Better Analytics and Reporting
For businesses with unique needs, bespoke payment processing software can be the ultimate solution. Unlike third-party platforms, custom software can be tailored to include any feature you desire to optimize your payment processes.
Expert Integration is Key
While payment processing offers undeniable advantages, proper integration is crucial. Partnering with skilled and experienced professionals ensures a seamless setup. A poorly designed or integrated system can lead to wasted time, financial losses, and damage to your customer trust and reputation.
Challenges and Solutions in Payment Processing Development
Building and integrating payment processing systems is no easy feat for developers. Here are the top challenges they face:
Navigating the Regulatory Maze:Compliance with ever-evolving regulations is a constant hurdle.
Staying Ahead of Security Threats:Fraudsters are relentless, so developers must continuously update fraud detection mechanisms.
Catering to a Diverse Payment Landscape:Offering a variety of payment options (credit cards, digital wallets, etc.) is crucial for businesses to meet customer preferences.
The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI-DSS) provides a framework for addressing security concerns. While this standard is a foundation, developers should go a step further and implement additional security measures within custom business solutions.
Conclusion
Payment processing systems are a double-edged sword. Seamless integration can be a boon for businesses, while a poor setup can lead to problems. The choice for your business boils down to two options:
Ready-made solutions:Platforms like Stripe offer ease of use and are ideal for many businesses.
Custom-built solutions:For unique needs, bespoke software can be tailored for optimal payment processing.

title: The payments ecosystem demystified | Medium
author: Ahmed Siddiqui
content:
Payments Ecosystem Overview
This is the introduction of a 4 part series on the Payments ecosystem. I plan on releasing one part per week for the next 5 weeks. A little bit about me: I’ve been working in the payments/fintech space for the last 6 years. I lead product for fintech startupBranch, and prior to that I was VP, Product over atMarqeta, a fintech unicorn. These are my personal opinions and are unrelated to Branch or Marqeta.
About a year ago, I came to the realization that not many people really understand how card based payments actually work. It is a complicated space, but my hope is that I can distill it down to parts so that entrepreneurs and software developers like you can understand what is all happening when a card is swiped. This lead me to publishing a book called“The Anatomy of the Swipe: Making Money Move” available on Amazonthat goes into the topic in further detail, discussing items such as banks, payment networks such as Visa and Mastercard, Issuer Processors, Acquirer Processors, trends in fintech, building a Neo-bank, and how understanding these concepts can help unlock the next “Fintech Unicorn”.
What’s needed to enable a card-based swipe?
The payments ecosystem can be complicated; however, it can be broken down into easily digestible pieces. When we talk about payments, we will primarily be referring to card-based payments. Before we get into our example, understanding a few key concepts will be helpful.
Fundamentally, four major things must exist for a card payment to work. Note: these same things apply for both credit and debit cards:
First, you need a card that is issued by a bank:
a. Sometimes it could be a physical piece of plastic with a magnetic stripe at the top and/or a chip.
b. Sometimes it could be a virtual card that is just the card number shown in an app, which can be used for online transactions.
c. Sometimes the card could be tokenized, meaning that it is a card stored in the phone’s wallet like Apple Pay or GPay and then used to “Tap and Pay.”
Key Term: Issuer
An Issuer or Issuing Bank’s function is to underwrite the user by giving them a bank account, a debit card, and potentially access to credit facilities and a credit card. Examples include Citibank, Wells Fargo, US Bank, and Chase.
Key Term: Issuer Processor
The Issuer needs a technology provider that can connect with the payment networks. Usually, the Issuer Processor will have a piece of hardware in their data centers and a fast network connection directly to the payment networks to approve or decline a transaction. Sometimes, the Issuer may have built this technology in-house or may rely on a third-party Issuer Processor to handle this. Examples include Marqeta, Tsys, Galileo, i2c.
Second, the Merchant, if they have a physical location, needs a machine that can read the card that is provided by an Acquirer:
Sometimes referred to as a card reader.
Sometimes referred to as a card terminal.
Sometimes referred to as a payment terminal.
Sometimes referred to as a Point of Sale (POS).
For online Merchants, this is referred to as a payment gateway. This isn’t a physical machine in this instance but rather it is handled via software.
Key Term: Merchant Acquirer
The Merchant Acquirer goes out and acquires Merchants and provides them the tools and facilities to accept and process card-based payments. Examples include Citibank, Wells Fargo, US Bank, and Chase.
Key Term: Acquirer Processor
The Merchant Acquirer needs a technology provider that can connect with the Payment Networks. Usually, the Acquirer Processor will have a piece of hardware in their data centers and a fast network connection directly to the Networks to request approval of a transaction. Sometimes, the Merchant Acquirer may have built this technology in-house or may rely on a third-party Acquirer Processor to handle this. Examples include Chase Paymentech, Tabapay, and Fiserv.
Thirdly, the linkage between the card and the card reader is the Payment Network, such as Mastercard or Visa.
Key Term: Payment Network
Sometimes referred to as a “Card Scheme” or just as a “Network.” Examples of Payment Networks include Visa, Mastercard, American Express, and Discover. These Payment Networks provide the rails for card-based transactions to occur. They sit in between Acquirers and Issuers and pass messages back and forth to make the transaction happen. The Payment Networks also set the communications rules and standards that the Acquirers and Issuers need to adhere to.
Lastly, a secure Internet connection for all of these messages to transmit back and forth.Now, this is done via Ethernet or even a Wi-Fi connection but in the past was done over the phone lines via dial-up connections.
To better understand the anatomy of the swipe, let’s look at an example:
Emmet is a young professional living in San Francisco working in the tech scene. He starts his morning off by taking a walk down the Embarcadero where he goes into San Francisco’s Ferry Building to buy a coffee at Bucks of Star Coffee. In his wallet, he has a Mastercard debit card from Moneybin Bank. He arrives at Bucks of Star Coffee in the morning. The Ferry Building is bustling with people getting on and off ferries with people scurrying off to work or getting on another train to continue their journey.
Something is magical about Bucks of Star Coffee’s mocha; the perfect temperature, the smoothness of the chocolate, and coffee that is slow dripped to make the perfect start to any day. Emmet buys a mocha for $4.75 and swipes his Moneybin Bank Mastercard at Bucks of Star Coffee’s payment terminal. When that swipe occurs, he sees the word “Authorizing” on the payment terminal. This typically stays in this state for three seconds or less, but within those three seconds, a lot is happening.
A message goes from the payment terminal to its Acquirer Processor with the amount of the transaction, location of the transaction, Merchant type, and the card number. The Acquirer Processor then determines that this is a Mastercard and routes it to the Mastercard Network.
Mastercard then sees this transaction and based on the card’s number, it looks for the first six digits of the card, also referred to as the card’s Bank Identification Number (BIN). Mastercard determines that this BIN belongs to Moneybin Bank.
Mastercard sends a message to Moneybin Bank with the card number, amount of the transaction, location of the transaction, and Merchant type.
Moneybin Bank’s Issuer Processor then looks at this data and makes a decision on whether this transaction should be approved. The key things it will ask based off of the information it has received from Mastercard are:
Does Emmet bank with Moneybin Bank?
Is Emmet’s card active?
Does Emmet have enough money in his account to cover the cost of this transaction?
Can Emmet’s card be used at this Merchant?
Does this transaction raise any sort of fraud flags based on location, prior activity, or type of Merchant?
If all of these questions get answered favorably, then Moneybin Bank’s Issuer Processor will send back a message to Mastercard that the transaction is approved. It will place a hold of $4.75 on Emmet’s account and the transaction will appear as “Pending” on Emmet’s statement.
Mastercard will then relay this decision from the Issuer to the Acquirer.
The Acquirer Processor will then send a message to the payment terminal to approve the transaction. The terminal then flashes the word “Approved,” and typically it prompts Emmet to sign for the order, or a paper receipt is printed where he can sign.
This transaction flow will serve as the basis for a lot of our discussion on the anatomy of a swipe.
So How Did Emmet Get His Card?
Emmet first needed to get a debit card for all of this to work. Issuers like Moneybin Bank distribute cards and underwrite the transaction on behalf of Payment Networks. The Payment Networks rely on Merchant Acquirers to get as many card terminals into the hands of as many Merchants as possible.
IdentifyingEmmet: KnowYourCustomer (KYC)
In this case, since Emmet was using his debit card, it is most likely that Emmet walked into the physical location of a Moneybin Bank (the Issuer) to open up a checking account. When opening up a checking account, Emmet was asked a series of questions that helped identify him. This is commonly referred to as the KYC process, or “Know Your Customer” process. In the US, the key means of performing KYC is by getting the following pieces of information from the user:
Name
Social security number
Date of birth
Physical address
Phone number
Potentially some other form of identification like a driver’s license, a passport, or government-issued ID
This is done primarily to prevent bad actors from entering the financial system. It checks to make sure that Emmet isn’t funding terrorist activity or hasn’t participated in money-laundering activities.
Once Emmet passes the KYC process, Emmet is then asked to deposit some funds into the checking account so he can start using his debit card or write checks.
Card Transactions Are Authorized by an Issuer Processor on Behalf of the Bank or Card Program Manager
Moneybin Bank uses an Issuer Processor to process transactions. In the case of Moneybin Bank, they have multiple Issuer Processors, but we’ll discuss at length some more modern Issuer Processors likeMarqetato understand how transactions are actually authorized and where opportunities lie.
Transactions Are Initiated by an Acquirer Processor Via a Gateway or Payments Facilitator
Bucks of Star Coffee uses Square for its terminal. Square is not an Acquirer Processor but rather a Payments Facilitator. We’ll talk at length aboutSquareand its capabilities as a Payments Facilitator and how it interacts with Chase Paymentech, its Acquirer Processor.
We’ll then talk about what it means to be an Acquirer Processor and opportunities in the space by looking at a modern Acquirer Processor,Tabapay. We’ll also look at some of the new technologies Acquirer Processors like Tabapay are offering to its customers.
The Card Networks Act as the “Rails” to Make All of This Work
Finally, we’ll do an in-depth look at Mastercard and where it sees card payments going. We’ll also talk about opportunities the Network is opening up for Issuers, Acquirers, and its consumers.
The next part to this series will be published on May 4th, please subscribe to my Medium page so you can be alerted when the next part is available. Also, if you would like to learn more about fintech, card based payments, payment networks, banks, and opportunities in payments, you may also purchase my book,“The Anatomy of the Swipe: Making Money Move” on Amazon.

title: Inventory Costing Methods Explained: LIFO, FIFO, and Weighted Average | by Muhammad Shaoor Nadeem | Medium

Inventory Costing Methods Explained: LIFO, FIFO, and Weighted Average
Inventory costing is an important concept in accounting that every business student needs to understand. Therefore, inventory valuation methods are used to figure out the cost inventory has and it also has a significant impact on the valuation of ending inventory, cost of goods sold, and gross profit on the income statement.
So today, I am going to share with you the three most common inventory costing methods — LIFO, FIFO, and Weighted Average. But before heading toward costing methods, there are some basics to be clarified about inventory costing.
So, What is Inventory Costing? in the First Place
Inventory costing refers to the method a company uses to assign costs to the units held in inventory. Since inventory is purchased at different times and different prices, the costing method determines which costs are matched with revenues to calculate cost of goods sold and gross margin.
Why Does Inventory Costing even Matter?
The selected inventory costing method impacts directly to the balance sheet and income statement. It determines the value of inventory assets and also affects the calculation of cost of goods sold and gross profit for the period. This in turn impacts net income and taxation.
The Three Main Inventory Costing Methods
There are three primary costing methods used for periodic and perpetual inventory systems:
1. FIFO: First-In, First-Out
The FIFO inventory valuation method assumes that the oldest inventory units purchased are sold first. Inventory value reflects the costs of the most recent purchases. Cost of goods sold is calculated using costs of the oldest units. Results in higher net income and higher inventory asset value.
2. LIFO: Last-In, First-Out
The LIFO method assumes that the most recent inventory purchases are sold first. Inventory value reflects the costs of the oldest purchases. Cost of goods sold uses costs of most recent purchases. Results in lower net income and lower inventory asset value.
3. Weighted Average Cost
The weighted average cost method averages the cost of units available for sale. Inventory value and cost of goods sold are based on the weighted average cost per unit. Results in moderate net income and inventory valuation.
When to Use Each Inventory Costing Method
FIFO is simple to apply and matches current revenues with oldest costs. It is commonly used by retailers.
LIFO better matches current revenues with current costs. It is utilized to reduce taxable income.
Weighted average is easy to understand and smooths out fluctuations in inventory costing.
Example LIFO Inventory Costing Problem
Let’s apply the LIFO method to solve an inventory costing problem.
Rana Furniture Factory had the following lumber inventory transactions in June:
June 1: Beginning inventory of 5 units at $16 per unit
June 5: Purchased 13 units at $20 per unit
June 19: Sold 9 units
June 23: Purchased 8 units at $18 per unit
June 30: Sold 12 units
Determine the ending cost of inventory on June 30 using the LIFO perpetual inventory method.
Solution:
Beginning inventory on June 1 = 5 units at $16 per unit = $80
Purchase on June 5 of 13 units at $20 per unit = $260
Sale on June 19 of 9 units removed from latest purchase:
9 units removed at $20 per unit = $180
Remaining inventory is 13–9 = 4 units at $20 per unit = $80
Purchase on June 23 of 8 units at $18 per unit = $144
Total inventory = 4 units at $20 per unit + 8 units at $18 per unit = $80 + $144 = $224
Sale on June 30 of 12 units removed the latest 8 units at $18 and 4 units at $20
8 units removed at $18 per unit = $144
4 units removed at $20 per unit = $80
Remaining inventory is 0 units
Ending inventory on June 30 is 0 units
Using the LIFO perpetual method demonstrates the flow of inventory costs and allows us to arrive at the accurate ending inventory valuation. I hope this article helped explain the key concepts behind inventory costing! Let me know if you have any other questions.

title: What is (FIFO) Method?. Introduction to FIFO Method | by Charles Manzoni | Medium

Introduction to FIFO Method
TheFIFO (First-In-First-Out) methodis an inventory valuation technique widely used in accounting and financial management. In this method, the first items added to inventory are the first ones to be removed or sold. Imagine a queue, where the first person to arrive is the first to leave; FIFO operates on a similar principle.
From a practical standpoint, when a company purchases or produces goods, the cost of the earliest acquired or produced items is assigned to the units sold first. This ensures that the cost of goods sold (COGS) reflects the most recent costs incurred by the business. FIFO is particularly relevant in industries with perishable or time-sensitive goods, as it mirrors the natural flow of inventory.
TheFIFO methodis straightforward and aligns with the chronological flow of inventory transactions. It provides a logical and easy-to-understand approach for tracking costs, aiding businesses in making informed decisions about pricing, profitability, and overall financial performance. While other inventory valuation methods exist, such as LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) and weighted average, FIFO remains a popular and widely accepted choice for its simplicity and adherence to real-world inventory flow.
Key Points of FIFO
There are several key points of fifo methods and here are some necessary key points given in the following:
FIFO, which stands for First-In-First-Out, follows the principle that the first items added to inventory are the first ones to be sold. In other words, the costs associated with the earliest purchases or production are allocated to goods sold before costs from more recent acquisitions.
FIFO provides a more accurate reflection of current costs in the cost of goods sold (COGS). This method assumes that the items remaining in inventory are the most recently acquired or produced, aligning with the natural flow of goods through a business.
FIFO is widely accepted and often preferred for financial reporting purposes. It is compliant with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) and International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), making it a suitable choice for businesses aiming for consistency and transparency in their financial statements.
The FIFO method is simple to understand and apply. It mimics the intuitive flow of goods in many industries and is particularly suitable for businesses with straightforward inventory systems. This simplicity makes it accessible to small businesses as well as large enterprises.
In periods of inflation, FIFO tends to result in a lower cost of goods sold compared to alternative methods like LIFO (Last-In-First-Out). This can be advantageous as it may lead to higher reported profits and reduced tax liabilities. Consequently, FIFO is often favored when inflationary pressures are a consideration for businesses.
Understanding FIFO Method
The FIFO (First-In-First-Out) method is a principle in inventory management that ensures the oldest units in stock are the first to be used or sold. It operates on the idea that the items received or produced first are the ones to be consumed or sold first, mirroring the natural flow of goods in most businesses. In practical terms, when calculating the cost of goods sold (COGS), FIFO assigns the cost of the earliest inventory on hand to items sold. This approach results in a more accurate representation of current costs, especially in industries where the chronological order of inventory matters.
One can envision FIFO as a queue, where the first entity to join is the first to exit. This method is straightforward, easy to understand, and aligns well with the chronological flow of business transactions. Its simplicity makes it particularly suitable for businesses with straightforward inventory systems. Moreover, FIFO is widely accepted in financial reporting and accounting standards, enhancing its credibility. In periods of inflation, FIFO can mitigate the impact on profits by assigning lower costs to goods sold, making it a strategic choice for businesses navigating varying economic conditions.
Calculating in FIFO Method
Calculating thecost of goods sold (COGS)using the FIFO (First-In-First-Out) method involves assigning the cost of the oldest inventory first. The formula for calculating the COGS under FIFO is relatively straightforward:
COGS=Cost of Oldest Inventory×Number of Units SoldCOGS=Cost of Oldest Inventory×Number of Units Sold
To break it down:
Identify the Cost of Oldest Inventory:
Determine the cost per unit of the oldest inventory in stock. This is usually based on the purchase or production cost of the earliest batch of goods.
Determine the Number of Units Sold:
Count the number of units sold during a specific period.
Apply the FIFO Formula:
Multiply the cost per unit of the oldest inventory by the number of units sold to calculate the COGS.
Example:
Let’s say a company purchases or produces goods as follows:
January 1: Purchased 100 units at $5 each
February 1: Purchased 150 units at $6 each
March 1: Purchased 200 units at $7 each
If 120 units are sold in March, the COGS under FIFO will be calculated as:
COGS=($5×100)+($6×20)=$500+$120=$620COGS=($5×100)+($6×20)=$500+$120=$620
This calculation reflects the fact that the first 100 units at $5 each and 20 units at $6 each were the ones sold, following the FIFO principle.

In this article, we’ll step you through the process whereby you will be able to prepare an accurate and meaningful cash flow statement use undirect method which as highlighted above gives you the financial direction of your business. No matter you are an entrepreneur, an accountant, or a financial analyst, this guide will enable you to prepare the cash flows statement in more understandable way, to present your financial reports that are both solid and engaging.
This article aims to demonstrate how to prepare a cash flow statement using the indirect method based on income statements, changes in capital, and increases and decreases from each account on the balance sheet. This article is also expected to provide an overview of the relationship between the profit and loss report, equity changes report, balance sheet, and cash flow statement which are part of the financial report.
The discussion in this article will be structured as follows.
Financial statement overview
Increase and decrease on balance sheet items
Income statement and changes in equity
Put it together into cash flow statement
Financial Statements Overview
This tutorial will use a set of financial reports published on the internet and Microsoft Excel as tools in preparing cash flow statement. The Un****er’s 2022 consolidated financial statements is used as a learning object on how to prepare a cash flow statement using the indirect method. Preparing a cash flow report using the indirect method requires an understanding of the relationship between the balance sheet, profit and loss and changes in equity.
If you interested to read the financial statements, it is available on thislink, and you will find financial statements in Excel spreadsheet file. It consists of balance sheet, income statement, changes in equity, cash flow and also notes to the financial statement. For this learning purpose please ignore the existing cash flow statement on that file, because we will try to preparing it from the income statement, balance sheet, and changes in equity.
Flashback to the first time worked at public accountant office in 2005, I have involved in several audit works for different business sectors and experienced in preparing financial statements. While preparing the statements, we always double check consistency of related items between statements. we make some check points as an indicator to make sure that the statements are already consistent.
After read the financial statements and their interrelationships, and apply checking mechanism as previously mentioned, we found something interesting fact, that the balance of cash and cash equivalents at the end of the year is not consistent between balance sheet and cash flow statement. The changes in cash and equivalent is not consistent also.
This error for some accountant may be seem not so significant for the readers, but this condition can be confusing, how to determine the actual cash balance, whether in the balance sheet or in the cash flow.
Increase and decrease on balance sheet items
The indirect method of preparation of cash flow statement begins with the net income at the top of the statement and then adjusts it with the changes in balance sheet accounts to get over from accrual accounting to cash accounting. The first step is to add all those non-cash expense to the net income that has been excluded, expenses such as depreciation and amortization expenses, which though they have been deducted in arriving at the net income were not actual cash outgoings.
Next, there is an adjustment for the changes in the working capital sub-accounts including accounts receivable, inventories, and accounts payable. For example, an increase in accounts receivable is subtracted because even though it contains money that a business expects to collect from its customers, this has not been realized as cash, an increase in accounts payable is added because it shows that a business owes money to its’ suppliers but has not paid this figure in cash yet.
This indicates the net operating cash provided or used which is derived as follows; This method is common because it establishes relationship between the cash flow statement and the income statement as well as balance sheet so as to facilitate comprehension of the effect of operating activities of cash flow.
That method requires to calculate increase and decrease of all of the balance sheet elements to be used as correction to the net income to reveal the actual cash inflow and outflow from operation, and also to calculate the cash flow from investing activity and financing activity. The balance sheet we have is already presented comparatively for year 2021 and 2022.
Hence, The first step in preparing cash flow statement is to calculate the increase decrease in balance sheet items. The increasing current asset other than cash and equivalent are deduction for the the net income as adjustment for non-cash transaction, for example increase in account receivable indicate that there are a part of the company’s sales that does not generate cash inflow. On the other hand, an increase in current liabilities indicates that there are expenses that have not yet become cash expenditures, so they need to be added to net income.
To make calculations easier, we create a difference column in the balance sheet. The difference in liabilities is calculated by subtracting the balance for 2022 from 2021, so that the increase will have a positive value and the decrease will have a negative value. Meanwhile, assets are calculated in the opposite way. We also mark each changing in balance sheet item as operating, investing, and financing activity.
When prepare the cash flow statement you need to remember the basic equation Asset = Liabilities + Equity, also for the changes. So, We could calculate changes in cash and equivalent is calculated from total changes in liabilities and equity minus total assets except cash and equivalent. That columns will be used to help ensure that increases and decreases on the balance sheet have been included in the preparation of the cash flow statement.
Income statement and changes in equity
Increase and decrease of equity in the balance sheet are explained more detail in the statement of change in equity. One of the item that change the equity is net income, also check that net income that stated is consistent with the income statement.
Put it together into cash flow statement
We prepare a cash flow statement by entering each of the difference in the balance sheet in sequentially manner from equity to assets, so it will be easier to ensure that all of the required items are entered correctly.
One by one, each changes in liabilities and equity have been entered into operating, investing and financing activity section in the cashflow statement. It could be check by sum all item and comparing the total with the total changes in liabilities and equity. It could be seen in the Figure 5 below.
we need to look at the notes on property, land and equipment because they are presented as in net value on the balance sheet, in these notes you can get the details and then separate the difference in historical cost of the assets and the difference in accumulated depreciation.
Separating what goes into operating and investment activities from the details of changes in assets and accumulated depreciation will actually be quite complicated, but in this section we will just simplify it that we enter all changes in accumulated depreciation on assets as operating activities in the cash flow statement.
Another account on the balance sheet that we must look at in detail in the notes is assets held for sale, because it includes both current assets and non-current assets that are classified as held for sale.
After calculating the increase and decrease in these details and determining the activity category, then enter it into the cash flow report and ensure the total value equal with the change in the assets held for sale account on the balance sheet.
After all changes in the balance sheet accounts other than cash and cash equivalents have been entered into the cash flow report, we can easily get the value of changes in cash and cash equivalents according to the increase or decrease in the balance sheet, this can be checked in the control column that we have added to the balance sheet.
The preparation of the cash flow statement using the indirect method has been completed, checking could be carried out to ensure its consistency with the balance sheet. As can be seen in Figure 9, the cash balance at the end of the period in the cash flow statement has been consistent with the balance sheet.
The preparation of cash flow in this article does not take into account all the details in the notes of financial report, so it is still possible that there may be errors in the categorization of activities. Considering that there are many details that must be considered to make the results closer to the results of the direct method, and that will be discussed in the next part of this article.
The excel file that used in this tutorial is available to download from drive, please clickhereto get that file.
Conclusion
In conclusion, preparing a cash flow statement using the indirect method is easy, the steps are clear and easy to do by understanding the increases and decreases in non-cash assets, liabilities and equity on the balance sheet and their’s relationship with the cash flow. It offers a summary of a company’s operating activities and its effects on cash flow. The indirect method of conversion of net income to operating cash flow is simple and effective because it begins with net income and incorporates the simplification that was made for non- cash items and change in working capital.
However, this method is very easy to implement and it does not allow user to get a clear picture of individual activities that either generate cash or consume it. As for those who have a finer detail into the solution, the next article continues to identify how to classify the items in the indirect cash flow statement, making it even nearer to the direct method of preparing cash flow statement.
Thank you for taking the time to read my article, I hope it is useful and please follow my account to get other interesting articles
